LADIES' LETTER

MY DEAR NELLIE, I have been quite delighted at the change the fashion has taken in regard to headgear. The weather is stil mild and I am afraid those toques would have come into fashion if we had bad a spell of wintry weather. Felt seems to be the prevailing fashion just now. I saw a hat which delighted me beyond measure the other day. It was an artistic hat of pale fawn beaver felt, which was so soft and pliable that the wide brim was folded up in a fantastic shape, and appeared to be held by a band of velvet which goes over the top of the crown, drawing:up the brim on either side. The trimming consists of beautiful natural- coloured ostrich tips which tone perfectly with the felt and the velvet. They are on the left side, one of them hanging thy.vn so as to come below the brim. In front of the crown was a bow of red ribbon, not too bright, and and this appeared to be flattened down to the hat by a paste buckle. The hat looked truly charm. kg, and I admired it immensely. The brim of the hat rose on both sides, and left sufficient room to show the wearer's luxuriant golden hair which she had arranged so neat and prettily. The bat locked very seasonable.

saw the other evening a beautiful long jacket -which a lady was wearing, and I thought it looked so very warm. The bodice was cut in a very plain style, yet the trimming on it was simply delight- ful. This consisted for the most part of a beauti- ful brown fur which ran right round the back of the collar and was continued down both sides ot the skirt th the feet. The garment was of a black silk material, but I could not get near enough the wearer to make sure of the material. I thought that a velvet cloak would be warm, but lam afraid that it would be too heavy, and I am sure I could not advise you to have one of that material. The cloak fitted the wearer close round the hips and waist, but was rather loose about the feet, gluing plenty of room for walking exercise. I thought the article a very sensible one, for, with proper care, I am sure it would last all through the winter. The lady, I noticed too, carried a beautiful fur muff, fiet in this case, too, I was not able, to identify the material.

The prospect of evening partss, dances and balls brii,gs to mini evenin,4 dvet.see. The bodices of ball arid &nos gowns are this 'F!On cut excep- tionally low—in fact, so low I hat folds of tulle, chiffon, or other ethereal fabrics are used to fill in the bodice, an:l these folds are aily -anged on the lining, and the bodice allo.ked to fail over them in tbe well-known pianofore fashion. Black bodices arranged in this style, with flesh-pink chiffon, have quite a startling etiect at a distance, the bodice appearing so extremely decollcti. While the long day sleeve has been growing closer and more condensed at the top, the short sleeve has almost disappeared, and in its place we have folds of chiffon, straps adorned with flowers or passementerie, or frills of lace about the shoulders and concealing a very tiny pufftql sleeve. Elbow sleeves are again fashionable, but have by no means eclipsed those long transparent sleeves to which we have grown attached,

I am pleased to hear that you are going to have -V,ia evening wrap, and please pet it at once, for you are needing it, I am sure. White or ivory cloth, smooth or dull-sulficed, would he the most fashion- able material for your eveninj wrap. Next to this comes a heavy make of cashmere serge is not often nserl. The cape should reach below the hips, fit closely roned the shoulders, and hang in full folds at the hem, the fronts heing rounded. Hoods are not very popular this season and I should advise you so make your cape without one, having a high stiffened collar prettily trimmed. You could border the cape with a shaped flounce of the material edged and beecicd with ruches of white satin ribbon or narrow hands of white fur or fea.ther-triemeimi ; or the film-me might be • dispensed with, and the cape made plain, and trimmed with several rows cf white ribbon

gathered slightly along the upper edges so as to form little frills. The collar should be edged with fur or feather.tzimming, however, unless you have a full ruche of chiffon or lace inside, finished with a bow and ends in front. Quilted linings are not so fashionable as those of plain silk or brocade, but you will need an interlining of domette or coarse flannel. Two thicknesses may be required if both cloth and silk lining are thin. Do not use a stiff material as interlining, or the cape will hang awk. wardly and be apt to crease. Your loving Jima.

div.p: " WOMEN'S CULT." The QUE,CII'B private sittin.,,-room at o,b nme is lofty aucl almost square in shape. The walls, in,tead of being as at Windscr,panelled in costly silk damask.are piiioly painted a pale restful green, while the ceiling is on- decorated, save for a large plaster centre oveame et, ar d a very simple cornice. The furniture is upaolstered in a very ordinary green and red flowercd chintz. of a pat- tern which has been a favourite with Her Maksty for many years. It is a very light and cherrful apartment, for an unimpeded view across the sea is not veiled with voluminous curtains, or shut lout by heavy blinds. The Queen's bedroom is large and airy, by no means overcrowded with furniture, all of which) is very homely , and substantial, the wardrobes being of mahogany, and the chairs and couches covered with the same patterned chintz as the sitting-room. The walls are painted salmon pink. The small mantlepiece,framing a highly-polished steel grate, %hie] glows all Christmas through with the beech-log fires the Queen so loves—is of white marble and severely plain. There are about fifty pictures on 1 the wails, two thirds of which are interesting from a purely family point of view, for they are principally portraits at various ages ef her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, sons and daughter-it-law, and

-c-tti—e7 relatives. By the way, the 25th of December has not always been the day fixed as that upon which Christ was born. Before the fourth century many people believed that April 20th was the eventful day, others May 20th, and in Egypt the belief prevailed that it was January 6th. St. John Chrysostom,in a Christmas sermon, preached on December 25th, 386. said that this thy had not been clearly known to them lonzer than ten years, '6 but it had ben familiar from th 3 beginnine to those who dwelt in the West." From thi. it appears evident that December 25th was, in the fourth century, adopted by the Church in the Esst, in conformity with the tradi- tional custom in Western Europe. The date of the cru- cifixion can be fixed with t,leratlo accuracy, but as a matter offset the sate of the nativity is abiolutely un- known. St. John Chrysostom, the most renowned of the Greek fathers, was horn of noble par. nts, A.D., 345 (,ome writers say 347) at Antioch, the capital of Syria. He was educated for the law. and studied oratory at AD.. ticch under the Paean Libaniue, who declared him worthy to be he successor were it not that the Chris- tian had made him a proselyte, and he spent some time in the schools at Athens. After a very succeslfut com- mencement of legal practic, he relinquished tire profes- sion of law for that of divinity. The works nt St. vstom are wry numerous. They consist Gf com- mentaries, 700 homilies, oration, doctrinal treatises, and 242 rpistles. 'The style Is diffuse, and over-loaded with mrtaphers and sirnilies. Fashionable f)lks are busy arranging for their flight south That. Christmas mu 4 be spent in their own land ard in their own or a friend's house, is one of the un- written laws, hut having done their "duty" they escape, at the earliest possible moment, t, the sunny Revives. The Reviera season is, as a rule, the harbinger of dress for the rpring tith 113. Dress for the spring, is dress for the year, aq to a certain extent the chief notes are sounded in it. Therefore the Reviera is a seasom of some

importance. Th. death of Baron Ferdinand Rothschild, and Mr. Chri,t Petrel. Sykes,has added considerably to the shadow which hangs over the Sandringham Christmas party this year. Both men will be terribly missed by all members sf the family, who regarded them in an affectionve manner. Very son now the Priece and Princess of Wales will botlitting South, and probably no one will be more glad than Her Royal Highness, when the present sca>on is over. In Buckinghamshire the Rothchilds hold several fine estates. Lori Rethschild has a magnificent estate at Ding, Mr. Leorold Rothschild is the owner of Ascot Hall, and Mr. Alfred Rothschild of Halton Hall. The late Baron resided at Waddesdon Manor, while the two splendid estates of Aston Clinton,acd Menton-Tr, belong respective!y to Lord Battersea, and Lord Rosebery, who both married daughters of this hovers. It is remarkable that Heitems do not even in the days whea land paid, seem to have hankered after it in this country, whe,eas in other countries they have had large pssseseions. With the exception of the Rothschild, there is probably no Jewish landowner in England who owns 10,000 acres and only two or three own half that quantity. MiS3 Alice Rothschild did not live, as has been stated with her brother the late Baron. When he bought Mad- drsden Manor she purchased the adjoining estate of Fgeherpe Priory, which she likewise transformed at an immense cost. The gardens and hothouses are superb, several of the latter being devoted to the culture of those lovely deep pink malmaison carnations, which are called " Rothschild." Miss Rothschild is a clever, well-in- formed woman. She affects usually a somewhat mass. culite style of dress, often walking about her gardens in a hat, and long coat that might have been borrowed from her brothers, for all one can tell. Years atm, light shades for winter wear, would have teen deemed impcsAle. But we have reserved this order of things completely. And pale delic,te tints, trimmed with fur or velvet are now worn in the morning as well as afternoon, and by middle-a,ged as well as the young. No longer need the woman on the shady side of fifty, or even sixty, appear in howdy rolourid gar- nriats. White, and light tones are permissible for all. which, provided they are carefully nosen, is a state of affairs to congratulate ourselves upon. A great feature of the smart bodice of this whiter is thei yoke, cot in one piece with th 3 epaulettes. It re- quirel neat cutt:og, to achieve success. Properly fashioned, it ai'apts itself specially to the pinafore style of gown, and s gain, equally well to the modified bolero. Indifferent eircas makers still persist in cutting the epaulette as a separate member of the bodice, and seam- ing it on at the shoulder, but such a mede of procedure should not be tolerated for a moment by the woman possessed of the Frilliest aspirations to be deemed rntdish. It i 3 much ea.sier to tell a wcmaie's caracter by hr dress, than by her handwriting, eipscially when ore takes icto cn-'s calculations the choice of color, which is co eloquent of good taste or the revere. l'he refined woman, the tidy woman, the vain woman, the vulgar woman, each betrays herself be the se': of a near, the arra h,gemerts of a bow, the disposal ci jewedery, and other accessrries, which reveal themselves to the obser- vant eve. The rich woman exquisitely dressed in the latest fashion, by a skilful French drwsmaker, will otters betray innate vulgarity as unmistakably to the discern- ing person, as her shabby sistc!. in humble garments re- veals her delicacy of mind and idea. The Germans have a proverb to the effect that a pretty woman leere,' to dress. It would be more strictly true to ray that a refined, tasteful woman is easily dressed. She knows exactly what suits her, and ho to pua it 03. A little

Why her example is not followed in London. Edinburgh' Dublin, and a few of the largest towns in these Isles, it is difficult to comprehend. Shopping by post is vete' unsatisfactory, and beside some people would benefit enormously by delegating their taste to a profassionil shopper, who had a fine sense of colour and form. div.head: TWO ADVENTS.
div.p: TWO ADVENTS.

While the morning star still lingers, Gleaming through the frosty air, Li3t we to the village singers In you ivied house of prayer. How our weary heart rejoices, As we catch the glad refrain; And we dream of Angel voices, O'er J udea's hills again. Passing wondrous was the story. Which those Angels uttered then. How the Lord of life, and glory, Had appeared to die for men. But to pious Shephe,ds only, Came the joyful tidings down, As they meditated, lonely, On the hills round David's town. And when dawns the hour appointed, Jesus will again appear, But his chosen ones anointed Only shall behold him near. Then his dead, from sleep awaking, With the living Saints shall rise ; All eternal life partaking, All to meet him in the skies. J. H. W. CLINDINNING,
W arrington.

div.head: JET OF MARK PEPYS.
div.p: JET OF MARK PEPYS.
,Y FRED J. PROCTOR,
of "Timothy Twill's Secret," "Jean Marlou," "Dr. Dobbs," Sm.

CHAPTER XX V. INDIAN TREACHERY. 01i) fell upon Mark's neck and pathetically muntred: "These, my kinsmen, are struck down to oPlase the anger of the Almighty. The penalty of my neglect hath fallen on the innocent. If Rana nd her people have perished then am I a solital deer in the land of desolation. I look to none lee but thee for protection. My heart is searedbut I would live for the love I bear thee, save f( which love I had ere now passed to the unknoh world. I know thou wilt not forsake me in my rent sorrow, and hence the joy of wedlock, for thhurden is lighter when we twain bear it." Mar caressingly soothed her, replying softly in Indianorl d "Thoa art mine, even though .the whole kuvn upon thee. For better or for worse w was naY)atli, and of my wealth thou shalt share till thend of thy days ; so good cheer." "Thy fond love gives me courage," she respond', with affectionate joyfulness, 'courage to face le worst. Let us press onward." "It ihn ugly omen," Mark whispered to me in English" that the nearer we approach the Golden Vale thgess recognisable are the bodies." At lA, standing on the highest dome, which was itse thickly covered with ashes, we directed our teloopes to the once fertile valley. The sight which 'it our gaze was awful in its severity. We saw a vit smoking plain, upon which the well- known times, spires, and mighty crags had been pitched i the wildest confusion. A flood of rough vesiculal lava had poured from the fiery height, overwheaing trees and city, and even now we could se the mighty volcano spouting molten rock. Ther conguration of the Golden Vale was com- pletely ianged, for it was now a hideous glen filled wia hot sulphur springs, lead-coloured slime, black holders, and charred forest trees. Hundreds of fissuri smoked, and even at the distance where we stoo, the air was still laden with noxious vapours. so far as we could judge, near the site of Enna's ,?alace, the hot water and spray from a geyser set to a great height at intervals of about five mintes. And down, down beiteath that black shroud ly tens of thousands of cultured Indians, whose 9'1.8 and sciences were the wonder of those who visi!,,d this people in their glory. WherOlive fully comprehended the destruction, and herrwn forlorn position, she wept bitterly, This said her from a serious illness. The grief 4 P6cos Ns overwhelming. As for me, I hap recourseto all those known subterfuges to presergy a InaolY demeanour, but tears rolled down rut cheeks i spite of my resolution. Olive's fall front high °Ate of wealth and power, her pathetic looke and unlippy isolation touched Mark's heart. "Oliv, my love," said he, soothingly, "I feay the calaiity is greater than we expected ;" anill then, olif reading thoughts that might naturally occur t( her, he added, with commendable firm- ness; " did not marry thee, darling, for thy riches, lut for thyself, for thy goodness of heart, for thin intelligence, and for thy comeliness. Nei didst ti, seeing thou wert heiress to Kana's throne ind treasures, marry me for my wealth. For loves sake I will cherish thee." After that my heart went out to Mark Pepys, and it As easy to see in Olive's face and eyes how his graious assurance had lifted the drooping flower fa it to enjoy the sunshine of love. Now t happened that I cast my eyes to the north-wt and saw strangers coming towards us. One of tiem, in Californian dress, was waving a white likdkerchief tied to a stick as a signal; so, without Sesitation, we made for them, more out of curiosity than with pleasure, as Olive was for explorini the whole outskirts of Golden Vale to find traqs of her people. Short lf coming up to the little band, to our joy we discovered they were some of the San Leno hands Ott searching for us. The meeting of such unexpected friends cheered us considerably, and when tit, had paid their respects to Olive, Mark ouestioted them. "Is (olden Vale completely destroyed? " "Yes" answered the spokesman. "I guess es how the whole tribe is obliterated, except a few shepheris an' messengers on distant errands. Hardly inyone within the valley escaped." "Whit is the extent of the eruption? "I rekon about thirty miles long by ten broad, tannin' nor'-west and s'uth-east, and cuttin' right through the heart of Golden Vale. Of course the dayastaton extends beyond that, so far ez the hot ashes go. The poisonous gases hey withered iromens% tracks of land. It looks as though the volcano has rallied before death, fer ez we passed to the tior'ard of it there were signs of speedy exhaustion. It'll be extinct in six months, like some others the old Indians hey pointed out to as." "Well, what about the ranches at San Leno?" The tpokesman shrugged his shoulders, and the others hesitated to speak. I looked at them keenly and SEnt dismay on their countenances. r "Is loather Otando all right ? " pressed Mark, earnestly looking from one to the other. "He's dead," frankly admitted the leader. . . "Killed in an attack by Muro's horde. The women al' children were spared, an' such men ea caved in," "Hood heavens, man!" hastily exclaimed Mark, "what d 1 you mean ? " "It's too true; an' the homesteads near Yerba Buena aliio are in the brigand's hands. We only escaped with the akin of our teeth. The cruel blackguaq has laid waste hundreds of miles of the best country; at least, he has the credit fer it, and but ter yon destruction he swore to revenge himself nt Kana for harb'rin' you." "The dead may yet rise in judgment against biro," sa‘d Mark firmly. "We Mist gang back to San Leno by the shortest route," I mggested as a feeler. "I reek% you'll go to certain death," replied the fer Muro has set a darned big price dead or alive." Mark froVned and clenched his teeth. "Muro will think I'm swallowed up in Golden Vale." But spokesman, yeesru hiaena, 4 ‘3: tlcle visitors mournfully shook their heads. .`Hope ez I don't presume," observed an old sr belonging 'to our northern ranch, "but my 'ig advice is this. I know the country perty to the tter'-west. We must work our way id over tile passes,. an' in a semi-circle fetch upper rataches of the Merced or Tuolumne is. The sPeed of our journey will depend on tveather, for the way to Mono is a well-beaten s p'tt ,\Ve're betwixt the 'Castilian's knife an' the qa mnyina part aal° I 0 choosehe mountains,"oface the lsaatitde r!.' gravely. " re you men positively sure," asked Mark, the eruption was so unexpected as to over- liana and her people ? " rall, I'm darned gosh cert'n," answered a L,,e, ccfer several who war on the fringe barely minit to run out of danger. The air Was atin'. One pore feller we met was horribly ied by the hot ashes, an' he told us how the Ler and lightnin' was thet dreadful. The trembled fer miles round, an' the wife of a man over thar to the sou-'west died from , in the arms of my pr.rd. Her husband was , city at the time. Depend on it not a scrap ,nn 's wealth is worth the huntin' for. Chaps, het right? " nodded, and another chimed in: "My r tells me he remembers a similar thing ez 'lied in Mexico in his young days. Why they y ez how rivers hey changed their courses, lakes disappeared, an' mountains risen in night. Thet may be hearsay, but this swing au of Golden Vale ain't gossip; it is a sight too real." k turned aside and conferred for some time is wife. Presently he announced that for esent they would avoid Muro. "By this on," I reasoned to myself, "he avoids a dual r, vengeance from Min.° and possibly retribu- from England." His determination gave 1 satisfaction, and just fifteen of us, exclu- f jip, formed the party. ore we descended by the zig-zag path Olive ore cast her eyes upon the valley, and the wing of her mind during that brief farewell is d human comprehension. is evident Muro means to exterminate us, ," observed Mark. "You see, he has gleaned was absent during the eruption, and will the country to cut us off, the monster!" a thought of the dangers to which we were Ling ourselves in order to avoid this evil genius nough to make the bravest quail. With a great before us, we needed stout hearts. ro doubt Muro has seized my private papers," „ed Mark. "I ars now practically thrown on

and tho wag forts TOP fino

my awn resources, and ray only b.ope XI to latch the border coastwards and establiiih este for reparatnis We must moye on at daybreak, bu the way is heavy and difficult." "The man o' courage rises superior to mis- fortune," I responded emphatically. "Look at yer wife's grit ; her mother an' tribe gone at one fell swoop, an' yeti Oliys doesna fret hersel' ill. That is heroism." _ _

Mark puffed at his pipe, looking at me from the corner of his bright eyes. "The icy opinion of the woman-hater is thawing," he chuckled. We promptly set out on our hazardous journey, when one afternoon Mark took me aside and said:

"Sandy, my food seems to turn on my stomach. I retch so much that I sometimes fancy I'm going to turn up my toes. Now, I wish to secure Olive from want; and to that end I've written some necessary information in my pocket-book." He patted his breast pocket. "If I should go off the hooks, old chap, take charge of this book, and do precisely as I direct. There is nothing but what an honourable friendship would dictate. It may necessitate your going to England. Will you pro, raise that so far as lies in your power you will ea,rry out my instructions ? " "Certainly," said I; and we shook hands, Mark pressing mine for several seconds. He then turned his head half aside, for the tears were welling into this stalwart man's eyes. I was reminded of a comrade's last wish on the field of battle. I know _ _

my own eyes glistened in the fireglow, for Mark's request was pathetically put. "Either he has some misgiving about his health," I mentally argued, "or he thinks Muro will strike him down unawares." "Don't drop a hint to my wife by word or look, for a woman is miserable until her curiosity is satisfied. Women scoff at the craft which keeps its secrets."

"What aboot the temptation t' me?" "Sandy, a trusty friend is incapable of dis- gracing himself by treachery; nor could you hope to gain by it. From now my lips are sealed." "Mark," quoth I in a tremulously suggestive tone, "I've noticed the last day or twa that ye lute scarcely eaten.onything. Are ye worrying because

we're a' penniless? " - He smiled, and glanced round to see that nobody was within earshot. "'Well, you see, as leader I am virtually responsible for your lives. Judas betrayed the Master for thirty pieces of silver, and it is not exhilarating to know that a handsome reward will be paid by Muro for my body." He gazed intently at a curl of tobacco smoke, and then added: "Herqdias demanded the head of John the Baptist. I used to wonder whether Lucia Diaz had pleased Muro, and named her price. . . I misjudged Lucia." The manner of delivery and decisive intonation of his words made my heart ache for him. But the subject dropped. We stifled dread by pushing onward, for delay meant annihilation. For some strange reason health declined day by day, and from the robust and stalwart he grew comparative le pale and thin. Once or twice a wicked suggestion crossed my mind—more horrible as it cropped up ao.ain and again. Was there not a tradition in Gorden Vale that the mutilation or robbery of the Royal dead would bring calamity upon all concerned in it, directly or indirectly? Was not revenge for such desecration a part of Kana's creed? Painful as they appear, I must record my thoughts. Olive was skilled in the knowledge of poisonous herbs, but for me to attribute anything diabolical to such a devoted wife Deemed inhuman. And yet I am ashamed to say I had doubts of her sincerity till an episode occurred which removed all 'doubts. Mark had grown almost too weak for the saddle, and she took me aside and said: "Rejoice, my husband will live! I have found the cause of his sickness. Be watchful of him while I search the woods for herbs; and if he needs fdocl, share thine with him. Let none else make nor give him food ; so shall the truth unfold itself. Be silent, and watch!

Strange to relate, from that day Mark began to mend; but two of the Indians—one of whom had assisted in cooking his food—gradually sickened and were like to die. This proved little, for they might be suffering from the epidemic caught by our respected leader. Like a smart woman, Olive had grafted to her nature the art of detection. She had watched over her husband with such fidelity that I welcomed any new phase to remove my pre- judice and suspicions. The finesse observed by her was beyond praise, and on giving the traitors a chance to recover and administer a noxious poison to Mark's food they took the bait and were caught. I was beginning to think that women are more discerning than men ; for Olive now received the food from our cooks and carried it to her tent, instead of us being severally and directly waited on stopesciiiait the llyfoNrViihleril Of e r nisblnthd. weredaceinrttayindliyshesstimrraede d, but not eaten; and Olive, pleading a like sickness with the Indians, refused hers. Now, our pro- visions running short, the red cooks greedily ate what Olive left, tut s7cretly scattered Mark's food among the brushwood and to the four quarters of the compa: , as a cunning safeguard against detec- tion. But the red men smelt a rat, and one morning ti ey did not return from a ramble, and we waited in vain for them to prepare our dirner. Meanwhile .11-ark slept heavily. Then si ake the cute princess: "The red men poisoned my husband's food that he might pine and die. But I set a trap, and fearing me, they have fled. The traitors are weak, and will faint by the way; for often I changed the food, and they partook of that which was poisonous. Let some pursue and overtake them; so shall the Lord smile at the punishment to be meted unto those who lust after gold, even to the destruction of the innocent. They would betray their master for the price set upon his head. Delay not, for 1 have spoken the truth. My lord is already on the mend." The herbs, then, which Olive had gathered, were an antidote, forcing the Poison from Mark's system and bracing him to renewed vigour. We scouted in parties of three, Jip guiding my trio—as right he should, for a keen-scented blood- hound would enable me to arrest the knaves. After about fifteen miles hard riding, and zigzag excur- sions right and left for communication with other parties, we came to a small forest, where a smouldering fire indicated a recent carousal. Tied to the trunk of a tree was one of our runaways, with his heart torn out and his body mutilated and drawn, as though he had passed through great tortures. About twenty yards away, among an underbush of hazel, lay the other Indian, scalped, and bleed- ing to death. In a ready fashion I stopped the blood flowing from several dangerous wounds, and when he was somewhat recovered, I said in the Indian tongue "Speak the truth, and I will not add to thy pain. Who kidnapped thee?" I "None. We fell into evil hands." "Thou didst flee, fearing the White Chief's wrath? " He nodded. "What motive hadst thou in poisoning my lord? " The price set on the White Chief's head," he spasmodically replied in great pain. "I am taken for death. 0 paleface, put me out of my misery." He muttered some incoherent sentences, writhing and groaning the while, and within five minutes expired without satisfying my burning curiosity about Muro's aim and whereabouts. We covered ' the bodies with leaves, and left them as carrion for the birds and wolves. Two lessons were suggested by this ugly incident : that it was wise for all of us to be silent concern- ing the poisoning, and that Olive alone should prepare Mark's food. I cannot speak in terms of praise too high for Olive. Her domestic virtues brought comfort in straitened circumstances. Thus, when the cold weather set in, and our buckskin garments became necessary, her housewife was an article of considerable value. Her aptitude as a needlewoman was appreciated all round. In an ill-assorted marriage I have known mutual aid bring content ; and whatever affinity there was between this couple was strengthened by the wife's devotion. The use to which our Princess put fir cones rather surprised me. In their virgin state these cones are coated with a gummy substance, render- ine, them impervious to wet, and preserving the seeds. Olive extracted the gum and mixed it with the juice of certain herbs. This she refined and rubbed into our buckskin, making it supple, strong, andi discovery oomvweoryii it touhfrae p-tphpreeonoelfan dai ba ontstt, hreraeceh ewr ye,e wk h at aftero n et he of our younger men wandered alone to "prospect" s quartz vein, and got mangled to death by some wild beast. There were evidences of a fierce struggle. We solemnly buried the poor lad, and erected a cairn to mark his last resting-place. This death east a gloom over our party; and until we had passed onward for some miles, it did not dawn on us that the cairn might act as a guide for our enemies. But it was too dangerous to return. We started for the beautiful coniferous forests, where possibly at that time no European had trod —for the sheepmen and miners, the Yosemite tourists, and the land speculators had not yet invaded this district of the Sierras.
SEM Authk.

Towne* noon the weather grew dull and cold, and by Ofteee o'clock we experienced the misery and saw the awful grandeur of a wind-storm. First there was the gentle cooling of a zephyr as it caressed the delicate ferns and made atender trees bend and kiss with ineffable grace. Then alarm- ing gusts beat upon the beautiful foliage as the birds sought shelter and the trees sang more lustily; and anon there came a calm more impres- sive than the doldrums. Then the horizontal arms of the kingly sugar pine began to swing round, and the sturdy Silver Firs to summon all their strength for a short tussle with the wind- fiend. Our party nestled behind boulders at a safe distance from those trees whose crowning foliage was likely to overturn them, like hobnails in pith which boys play with. The hurricane increased until trees were uprooted, streams lashed into fury, twigs, leaves, sand, and even stones flew past us with surprising velocity. The wind made terri- ble havoc in our camp. Our ponies were struck, garments carried over the heads Of patriarchal trees, and our breath almost taken away whenever we raised our heads. We shouted at each other, but to venture into the open was madness. The Vikings never experienced windstorms of greater pressure, for the feathery pines bent nearly to the ground, and the steadfast monarchs of the forest rocked from crown to base. The hurricane at last spent its fury, and then the swishing and swirling of the pines and the swaying of bushes sounded like the music of a thousand /Eolian lyres. Ms giants had struggled, and were being lulled to but not so Muro, who hovered about our patL a'voracious vulture. The elements alone hindered him from attacking us; still he was greedy for his prey.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVI.

. STONY HOLLOW. ' Now the storm gave a delightful freshness to everything, the rain o,,epening the colours of bark, dead firs, leaves, and ferns, just like an old ' painting cleaned and touched with oil. The moss- . greens and lichen-greys blended with the rock r colours, and the whole air was suffused with del i- P cate fragrance. Presently the woods began to throb 1 with life. Squirrels, which had rocked in their .dry nests, issued forth to admire the glinting raindrops kissing the lips of lovely autumn flowers ; birds, which had hopped under shelter, now began to chirp and peck as the big drops fell from the flower-cups upon the sodden turf. Every drop of rain was a merry messenger of goodwill, making the lion Sequoias feed with thankfulness, and the flowers smile as queens of beauty on May Day. And there, upon the mountains, our alpine Princess told us she would live for the living—a fairy among brusque men, an artist to shape the rough-hewn into a more pleasing image of divine

Mark had taught his wife our English alphabet, and I had used the kindergarten system in applying the word-sounds to concrete objects. Then by degrees we managed to associate ideas with thingb, not attempting too much nor wearying her. esteemed and honoured Mark for the consideration he shewed. and instead of an encumbrance Olive became a blessing to our party. On and onward we went, across wild gardens, ferny brooks, willowy streams and boggy meadows; emerging from isolated groves, wending over billowy rocks, mounting granite ridges, and through patches of evergreens, anon entering deep canons, and then passing out through lateral gorges ; pressing ever onward, right into the ice-peaked highlands. I would stake my existence that Muro could not reach us here, but I little dreamt of the greed of this monster for his prey I Now after many days came the wintry blasts, bringing to our minds the Indians' warnings, which in our conceit we foolishly unheeded. The ice-sheets upon the range began about a mile from the edge of the timber line, where we encamped with considerable forebodings. Our men named it Stony Hollow, for the pines were scarce and VOulders abounded. Mark called us together and said: _ _

"Prepare winter quarters, for here we stay. Make a pine your tent pole, and heap up a semi- circle of stones around it. All the available canvas and skins must be tied to the rafters, which you may secure to the pine and slant on to the wall. At the top leave a hole two feet square, and on the south side of the trunk, the entrance being on the same side. A corral, similarly built, but without the canvas, must be erected, large enough to tether all the ponies. Both houses can be built dome-shape after running vertical for five or six clear feet, branches being used at angles to support the pressure inward." "An' what aboot yoursel' ? " I asked. "I will build a cabin, using yonder rock as a side. We shall have to work almost night and day for a week. The occasional showers and sleet nay make the task somewhat unpleasant, but fuel, fish, and game must be stored for any emergency, and at once."
"What are our duties?" I inquired, waving my hand towards Pecos.

"Both of you must fish, trap game, and bring down edible birds. My wife will dry whatever you bag—that is, after our daily wants are satisfied. Three good shots must act as hunter-scouts; report- ing hostile Indians. I shall remain here as an amateur architect. At the least sign of danger a succession of blasts on any mountaineer's horn will be the signal for closing in, each man repeat- ing the warning as best he can. We builders will advance to cover your retreat." There was no danger from the north, because the end of our plateau rose in a succession of ridges to a great mountain whose patriarchal sum- - mit was the abode of perpetual snow and ice. But such precautions as we took were absolutely neces- sary, for, as Mark observed privately to me, "Muro is vindictive and unscrupulous; he'll brave any danger to hunt us down." "He'll die like a dog in a ditch," said I, grinding my teeth. "Every hellish trick is atoned for suner or later. He'll ne'er be a penny above a beggar, fer a' his swag' gangs to purchase popularity—mercenary fame, rotten at the base, an bound to totter an' fall!" Mark tapped my chest with his forefinger, saying: "Muro's offer of a reward for my body, dead or alive, is the source of our danger. He knows he must cut off our retreat, for if I get the r ear of the Government his prestige is gone." "He has Britons to cope wi' noo. We must be like marmots in winter quarters, hard t' find an' tough t' handle." Now I scouted for game, and about noon on the third day I was strolling down a ravine which ran from .Mark's Peak towards the west, when I dis- covered in the far distance three persons on horse- back, slowly moving up a trail towards my rendezvous. Fearless as a mountaineer's life had made me, inured to uncommon hardships for months, yet this sight made my heart beat with I excitement. "I must secure a safe passage home," thought I, and with that aim in view I buried my game and mounted the dizzy crags to a spot where a crevice in the granite enabled me to spy the intruders free from observation. Two tedious hours passed before the trio reached the dell beneath my crag. On arriving there the woman dis- mounted. The two on horseback were Indians, dressed in buckskin leggings and coats. They appeared peace- able enough, and the squaw, without the slightest hesitation, began the difficult task of climbing into my eyrie. Higher and yet higher came the stranger, surefooted and fearless, now resting to take breath, now lost to view underneath a hanging cliff, and then emerging upon a field of granulated snow. After a while she reached my camping- place, and carefully examined every square yard. I saw her raking the embers, hooking about the twigs and leaves, and then turning up the snow, loose ice, and rock-chips covering the carcases of my sheep. Her companions remained below, presumably obedient to her orders, and after a while she took out a telescope and made a long and thorough survey of the country. Pocketing her glass, she again examined my footprints, and, to my astonish- ment, selected the most recent for her trail. Save for an alpine staff, she appeared to have no weapon of defence. "If her mission is a friendly one," thought I, "I'll save her an unnecessary climb; if she be a mortal enemy, I have the advantage." So, placing my gun against the rock, I stepped two paces into the open, and waving my cap, shouted down with a clear, shrill voice: "Welcome, lady!" She drew up with a startled exclamation, and m catching sight of me waved her pocket-handker- chief, beckoning me. Seizing my gun with an assurance of safety, / walked steadily down the steep mountain side. "Friend or foe," I murmured, "surely I'm a match for a wuman." While I picked my road carefully the visitor sought a curve in the mountain where we could meet free from observation of her allies-below, and go for fully ten minutes we were unable to scan leach other but when we obtained that view both Of us stared with astonishment. I could see by her laughine eveet and delicate smile that she half-

understood my litter amazement ; and, forsooth, I was conscious of standing dumbfounded and scared. My knees trembled as I gazed at her, for there stood a woman the very image of Lucia Diaz! I thought for a moment that the dead waalan had risen! She placed her hand to her lips, tead made signs tor me to approach wirnom aistortm)g those below. You may be sure I looked at her in mingled wonder and fascination, for the situation was uncanny. Since Lucia made meat for the crabs, this was surely a water kelpie! "Try again," said She in Spanish, may recollect where last we met." "It seems to me," I stammered, "as if the resurrection has taken place, or my senses are clean gone! You are the very spit of one known to ;lark Pepys, and to his wife Princess Olive, as 'cliorita Lucia Diaz!"
"and you

-!-.e mention of Mark's name she aighed— „,i proved her mortal ; at the utterance of Olive's name she puckered her lips and knit her brow—which proved her a woman; and when I reiterated her own name, she put her finger to her lips, and said hurriedly: "Hush! There is a curtain between me and the past which would destroy my peace if it were lifted. I am indeed Lucia Diaz, once loved by Mark Pepys " ; and she added cynically: "in whose heart Olive the half- caste Princess now reigns. I wish him joy of his choice—a joy which by look, word, or deed I shall never break in upon. Tell me about them." I gave her the history of our hunt in San Francisco and other towns, of the hanging of Dolores, and Mark's sadness at being too late to save her.

"Dolores," she explained, "was considered my rival. Faugh Her imitation was crude, but yet she thought herself a musician and a woman of surpassing beauty. We might have been taken for twin sisters. She haunted the saloons when I broke from gay associations to settle down in the country. Lucky for me that Dolores aped the real Lucia Diaz. She was bad at heart, and I never deserved her fate." "We were deceived by the description given of Dolores. But why are you here? " "Aha!" she gaily replied. "Whence comes Lucia, and why? Fortune favours the bold, and iourney hither for a great stake. Are we alone?" Absolutely," I responded, ,smilingly. Her —...ety was allayed, for now I saw how she was struggling to suppress her inward emotion. "My confidence needs your solemn promise never to divulge the name or sex of your informant. Are you willing to abide by this restriction? " "It depends upon the nature of the confidence; for if it endangers any one of our party, I must Rot listen further." "Think you I should run such danger for wanton mischief? " she curtly asked, her eyes flashing with indignation. "My mission is to save you all from destruction. Are you convinced of my sincerity now ? " "Proceed, Senorita," I quietly responded, notic- ing the tears dimming her eyes as she gazed upon my weather-beaten face with some misgiving. "You must leave future action to my judgment; but this I swear—nothing shall escape my lips to make your confidence recoil on you." "I am weary," she sighed—"yet every moment is precious. Is Mark alive and well? " "When last we saw each other, yes." "How long since? " she asked anxiously. "Several days. lam hunting for food, as our people are starving." "Where are they?" she nervously asked. "Yonder, bearing south-east." Lucia sighed as she placed her hand on her palpitating heart. "Then Muro has scented his prey! " she exclaimed, her whole body quivering with agitation. "Go hack and warn Mark of his langer before it is too late!" "What proof have I that you are not playing us a trick ? "

"Fool!" cried she, the colour mounting to her cheeks in a moment. "D. you not see that I am in earnest? What selfisl motive can prompt me to risk being shot? " "You were the instigator of the plot which gave Muro access to the Golden Vale caverns, enabling him to rob Kana of the bodies of her Royal ancestors, and placing us all in jeopardy." "II shewed Muro this secret entrance to Golden Vale! What knave lied so foully ? " said Lucia between her teeth. "Be he who he may, name him, that I may deny this accusation to his face!"

"Your pardon, Senorita," said I. "One infer- ... ence alone could be drawn from the fact of you • knowing the entrance to the caves." .4 "Had I turned traitor, as you ungraciously-' assume, Muro might have stolen into the heart of : Golden Vale in the dead of the night. So disabuse : your mind at once of suspicion. With all my ' faults I am not capable of anything so diabolical. ' There is now no time for explanations, or prying,' into motives." "Have you not been in league with Muro, for ..., , ..., Mark's destruction?" "No—and the question is an insult! Side issues!, are sometimes more powerful than direct influences. Mark jilted me for Olive, the half-caste!—the ' tighter of a defunct tribe! She had prospects of, great wealth and rower—l bad none. Now she i* penniless, while I am rich—and money always' commands power." She laughed, and added: "The pendulum has simply swung the other way." .• "Senorita, I fear you are revengeful." • "And base as well? The prejudiced see things' with a squint. Listen, Senor Dees," she con- tinued, deprecating by gesture my attempt to interrupt: "the past is wiped out, as figures from a slate; and as you respect Mark Pepys, so r , charge you not to mention me. It is Muro's - intention to humble your chief ,if by stratagem - he can take him alive. Already his men hedge you in on every hand, save at this dangerous northern , side. I saw the glimmer of your own fire in yonder t copse the other night, and guessing someone from your camp was out hunting, I ventured here with two trusty guides. Lest you should run short of provisions, I will organise a hunting-party to- , morrow, and stop for a hasty meal in the woods where you sleep. Should there be a disposition for our party to climb higher, I can make sudden ' sickness an excuse—that is, if a feigned illness for such a cause is not sinful," she added sarcasti- cally; "but I will contrive to leave a good supply of tea, coffee, and extracts behind. My head- quarters are but three hours' journey to the west, ' at the end of yonder canon. It leads to the Tuolumne Meadows and Lake Ten-ai-ya." Anxious for information as to our exact position, . asked: "By following the left side of this range northward, shall we strike the Mono Pass? " "Yes; the trail cannot be more than twenty miles north," she answered, perceiving my object was to escape by this route; "but the way is rugged and dangerous, subject to river floods and fearful - storms." "Better die in the arms of nature," said / Philosophically, "than fall into the clutches of • Muro. By the way, Mark trusted Harry Puke. . Was the tavern-keeper faithful? "I have not been to Yerba Buena for months," was her speedy reply. "And you are not justified • in making me the keeper of other people's con- •? , sciences. "Why has Mark such an aversion to return to England?" • "I was not aware such a thought troubled him," '• she replied; and approaching a pace or two, she , coaxingly added : 'Tell me all about it." But I ' shook my head, and she winningly said: "Come, now, Senor Dees, your Scotch bluntness always ;, amused me, but never annoyed. The risk I run,' ' to-day proves my desire to protect him. If harml threatens him in England, let me share the secret, I 4 that I may befriend him. What has Harry Puke to do with it? You shake your head, and will ' not reply. Well, I must—l will ferret out the ' trath myself! i "?rudence demanded my silence, so thanking the isenorita for her advice and warning, I bid her eu. Her last and special injunction was this: -- .. bind you to your word not to mention me; but , urge Mark to escar,e at orre, even at the sacrifice • of the ponies and cal. Ting 'tear. Muro is slyly' but surely surrounding bin: and if you do not : warn him quickly, the whole of you will be -, massacred. There is not a moment to be lost. Go! God speed your footsteps, and save Mark repys I -----
(To be continued.)

div.head: WEIRD WOOING;
div.p: A WEIRD WOOING;
OR, THE GHOST-GUARDED TREASURE
A Tale of an Old-Time Christmas and New Year's Days. Er JAMES S. BOF.LASE, Author of "Darker than Death, "Riches to Ruin,* "An Ocean Secret," "Recalled to Lsfe," "The Shadow of the Knout."
CHAPTER I. THE WEIRD WOOING AT ST. ANTHONY E CHAPEL.

MR Christmas Eve, which fell on the Fifth of January, 1748, was, even as far north as Edinburgh, as mild and sunny as many a May Day; yet that was not the reason why Ivor Oliphant had begged Muriel Drummond to meet him at St. Anthony's ruinous chapel (which still stands at the base of Arthur's •Seat, looking across what is now the Queen's Park, towards the grim and yet stately old palace of Holyrood) but because her stern, mercenary father, Sir John Drummond, had forbidden him admission to his mansion in the Canon gate, as being a pardoned "rebel," whose already deeply wort gaged estates had been confiscated in consequence of his having drawn his sword, on the losing side, during the Civil War of 1745 and 1746.

This the young gentleman had done not -so much out of loyalty to the gallant, but ill-fated Chevalier, as in the hope that he would thereby win name and fame and owealth that, united, would make him more ,worthy of the hand of the beautiful girl whom he idolised rather than merely loved, and whose constarkcy he believed, at the time, no misfortune could shake.

, Alas, he had had, of late, grave reasons for doubting her once as firmly believed—in- fidelity, and he had sought, entreated, aye, even prayed for the coming interview, in order to put it to a final test. And yet he looked AS handsome, frank, and debonaire a young fellow as ever won a Woman's heart, and kept it through weal and woe; for he was tall and stalwart, fair of complexion, and perfect of feature, with laughing blue eyes, a pleasant smile, a soft voice; and, best of. all, a dauntless heart.

-There was no smile Upon his lips, or laugh- ter in his eyes upon the present occasion, however, for he had come to St. Anthony's Chapel to know his fate—to learn from the girl whose love he still felt sure he had once possessed, whether the rumour was true or false that she had, at last, yielded to her father's commands, .and consented to marry old and ugly Sir. Ralph Restalrigg, whose enormous wealth was the only recommenda- tion he possessed. The lady was already late at the tryst. In the early days of their mutual love she had never kept him waiting half as long as she was doing on this, he began to believe" ill-starred occa,sion ; so he shook his head, (which was crowned by the well powdered tie wig and triple cocked hat of the period), sadly. and dejectedly, as his moody gaze wandered over The "Hunter's Bog, and St. Margaret's Loch in turn, and hummed in low tones:
"Now Arthur's Seat shall be my bed, Saint Aigton's Well my drink shall be, Since my true love's forsaken me."

as sad of heart the while as had been the jilted lover who composed the words and gave them their pathetic tune on that very _spot a hundred :years and more ago. Presently, however' the expression of his face entirely changed, for two men, bearing a sedan chair, had suddenly turned the shoulder of the hill from the direction of Dunrappie's Loch, and come to a halt beside the clear, for 'ever up-bubbling waters of Saint Anthony's well. Ivor Oliphant at .once darts back into the little chapel ruins, for its strikes him that Muriel Drununond may not wish her chair- bearers to know whom she has come hither to meet; and there he plays nervously with the hilt of his sword until, a couple of minutes later, there entered the chapel in turn a young lady of some nineteen years of age' and so wondrous lovely that the man might well have been excused for the com- mittal of any ant of folly whilst under the influences of her charms. She was as dark asher lover was fair, with ;mat star-like eyes, that could be as soft as moonlight or as dazzling as the lightning's flash; her figure was perfectly and somewhat voluptuously proportioned, her skin wonder- fully clear, her features most delicately chiselled, her lips ruby red, and her teeth Of ivory whiteness; but there were times when, influenced by sadden and violent anger, the latter would bite the former till little beads of blood rose thereon • for, though so lovely to outward seeming, Muriel Drummond was haughty, self-willed, passionate, and, worse than all, intensely selfish. Some of her female friends called her, a•mongst themselves, " _The Leopard," and sae certainly possessed the innate ferocity of that animal, as well.a,s its outward beauty and grace of motion. There was much of that grace about her now, as she advanced towards her lover with both hands outstretched, at the same time saying; "Well, here I am, you see, though why i.you subjected me to the pain of again meet- ing you I cannot tell for the life of me. You know that I love you, Ivor; but with no chance of your ever beingable to afford, to marry me what is the use of our carrying ,on our pitiful little comedy any further ? " "If you really loved me, Muriel, you could inot speak to me in such a tone and way." "I do love you, though, and with one solitary exception, better, aye, much better than I do anyone else in the world." " And'the solitary exception is, I suppose, •old Sir Ralph Restalrigg, with whose name •all Edinburgh has lately taken to couple ,your own ? ' rejoined the young man, :bitterly. "No, Ivor, the exception is myself. I love myself better even than I do you, and so I have, at last, made up my mind to marry Sir Ralph Restalrigg, solely because he can bestow upon me all that my love of luxury .and ,pleasure have taught me to regard as essentials to my happiness." "Muriel, I have tried hard to win wealth for your sake." " I know it; but then, you see, you have failed:"

a.-es.c• "You would once have gladly .shared com- parative :poverty with me. Oh., why did I not then urge you to do so? ." Because you: thought more of my wel- fame than :you did of your own happiness. Ahl I was worth winning in those days. A young girl .of sixteen has, in general, very few limits; ;but God help such an one lairee years later, if she becomes motherless and possesses a father such as mine." Here tears tilled the lovely speaker's eyes, and full of pity, Ivor Oliphant would fain have folded her in his embrace and kissed her fondly, had she not eluded him. "Isle, Ivor, no," she said, in sorrowful cones. "With ll my faults lam still pure; so I will not allaw even you to press lips that of right now belong to another. I have told you what I really am M order to show you bow little you lose in losing me." "By the light .of heaven I have not lost you yet, nor .tIO I intend to do so until I have made one more determined effort to win you. Alas, had poor Prince Charley but succeede.d in recovering his father'n throne I should, ere now. have been the owner of unmortgaged lands, and, most probably, of a title as well." '4l warned you, IVor, when you joined the Prince's standard; that six feet by two of English or of Scottish soil was the sole amount of land that you would ever win in his service; a service you entered as Master of Oliphant, and quitted a pennils and prescribed adventurer. Thank heaven that

you had not to pay the further penalty of losing your head upon Tower Hill.' "That That matter is an old song now, Muriel, so I prithee to sing it no longer. There is, however, a path to wealth still lying open before me, and I mean to tread it this very night," responded our hero, determinedly. "Not the road, Ivor! Oh, not the road.!" exclaimed the fair girl, with a shudder, " for, though it is a gallant calling enough, and followed nowadays by many young men of good family; nor is there, that I can see, any lack of honour in pursuing such a career iso long as blackmail s only levied upor Whigs and such like, yet the highway so often leads to the gibbet, that—" "I was not thinking of adopting the profes sion of a highwayman, fashionable though it has become," exclaimed Oliphant, laughingly interrupting her. "No," he added, suddenly becoming grave again, "but there is an old building in Edinburgh which is supposed to be crammed with wealth, belonging now to no one, and yet which it would require a bold and even well-nigh desperate man to appropriate, for the house I speak of has been closed, barred, bolted, locked and sealed for more than a hundred years, and the Plague lies bwried therein."

" No, O, Ivor, it was not the Plague but Death himself who was buried a century ago in that old house in Beth's Wynd." "Death himself? What on earth do you mean, Muriel? For whoever heard of Death being of the masculine gender ?" exclaimed - Oliphant. "Listen and you shall hear, for my great aunt on the mother's side, Mistress Eldspeth Macfarlane, who died in her hundred and sixth year, when I was a little girl of nine, was herself a little girl at ti period of the great pestilence, and told my mother the tale of that old house in my presence, as I will now tell it to you, in order to kdeter you from the desperate enterprise which you seem to contemplate." "Tell it me, then., though mayhap it will only strengthen m.y resolve," answered 011. pliant, with scornful laugh. • "Well, when the fell disease was at its height, and floated about in the air in the shape of little golden-hued serpents no thicker than hairs; when huge bonfires blazed in every street to combat the awful stench of human corruption, and wherever two thoroughfares met a g.ibbet was set up whereon to hang any and all persons who managed to escape out of a house the plague had entered, and each one of which was • branded with a great red cross painted on its front door, Death, owing to his countless victories over life, won the power of incar- nating himself, that is to say, of assuming a human form, a tall, gaunt, livid-faced man, wearing a broad-brimmed black hat. slouched down over his forehead even to his eyes, which gleamed like live coals, and, draped in ,a long, loose horseman's cloak, reaching to his feet, he entered every house wherein the infected lay at their last gasp, in order to bear their souls away." "Go' on, Muriel," urged Oliphant, with a ghastly smile, as the girl at this juncture ,came to a panting pause, owing to being well-nigh overcome by the horrors she had conjured up. - "Of course," .she continued, with an effort. -" whenever Death entered no one ventured to oppose him, and few were bold enough even to look at him; but the, idea at last occurred to .a few that he might be privily followed to some house or other, and secured therein, so that he could do no further harm, and, eventually, he was, one night, so followed, and., happily, imprisoned in that old mansion in Beth's I,Vynd, where, at the time, the only remaining doctor in Edinburgh whom the Plague •had spared, lay in his last agony. Well, a guard. was instantly set at the front and back doors, and withinan hour those doors, and every window as well, were boarded over, and _sods were even laid atop -of all the chimneys. The next day the wood-work was well tarred 'over, as it has been twice a year ever since. The Plague suddenly • ceased it ravages so soon a-s Death was thus made captiVe, but a dread Uul curse will .as6ureelly fall npon that individual who opens his prison and lets him forth, most probably to bring the awful pestilence amongst us once more. Oh, Ivor, Mr God's sake, be not thou that man 1"
"Muriel, your Story makes no mention of the treasure."

"That was so unimportant an item com- pared with the others that I did not intro- duce it into my narrative. You must know that Doctor Davie Duncan, whose soul Death Was .going for when he was trapped, and for- 4sver, it is to be hoped, made captive, was a man whom every one revered for his probity and honour, wherefore nearly all the plague- stricken whom he attended confided their gold, jewels and plate to his care, lest they should be stolen by the drivers of the corpse- carts, when they came into their houses for their bodies, to convey them, uncoffined, and merely wrapped in the blankets whereon they had died, to the plague pits, wherein hun- dreds were interred before the yawning gulphs were covered over—But what are you Laughing at now, Ivor?" "I was laughing, Muriel, at the credulity of mankind, and at that clever fellow who. frightened people into the belief that he was death incarnated. Why, can't you perceive, as clearly as I do, that he must have been a common thief, who went into dying folk's houses, not for their souls, but for their gold and plate? Under that long, loose cloak of his he could carry away any amount of booty, and he knew well enough that his sombre get up, and his fictitious character, would frighten everyone from molesting him. Ah, he doubtless hoped to make a fine haul at Doctor Davie Duncan's. Of course, the fact of the plague subsiding so soon as he was effectually bottled up was a mere coincidence, for, in all probability, the pestilence had by then worn itself out. Well, the Doctor and Death, as you dub him, are still in possession, I reckon, though reduced to mere skeletons by this time, I should say. Happily the treasure must be there also, and that treasure shall become mine ere the rising sun ushers in another day." "The treasure may be guarded and de- fended by the ghosts of the two dead men, Ivor ? "

"Now, out upon your old world supersti- thin, though, even if it were so, a couple of live men, armed to the teeth, would better guard it, against rue than a dozen ghosts. Muriel, my own darling' I will win that treasure, and through the treasure your own most adorable self. -What say you ? Is it agreed ? " "If you are quite sure that "the Powers of Darkness will not be mired up in the matter, it is agreed, Ivor." "The darkness of the night will be the only darkness to be dealt with, my own darling, and that will be friendly instead of adverse. Come, bear a stout heart, and also quickly get you gone, for I have much, to see to ere night arrives. Old Sir Ralph Restairigg may now go whistle for a wife, whilst I will win the fairest and bonniest in all Edinburgh. Kiss me, Muriel, for, as matters stand, you may do so with a clear conscience. Kiss me and then away. To- morrow I will call at your father's house in Canongate, and demand of him your hand in marriage,- without the slightest fear of being again turned from his door." Carried , away by . her hiv4m.'s sanguine hopes, .and her own real affection for him, the kiss was given, and then Muriel Drum- mond ran down the hillside, and re-entered. her sedan chair, to be borne swiftly away. The weird wooing was ended, but the most woful wedding ever chronicled .r.-.as vet to come.
CHAPTER IL
THE GHOST-GUARDED TREASURE IN BETH'S
WYND.
LET not the reader suppose that our grue- some Christmas story is far-fetched'' and improbable, for, on the contrary, it has the merit, if merit it iv, a being as true as it le strange.

In proof of how long-lived and hard to kill superstition is, we may here add that when the old house in Beth's Wynd, which, in imagination, we are now about to enter, was pulled down in the year 1808, to permit of the Advocate's Library being erected on its site, it was still furnished exactly- as when the Plague had visited it in 1615, and all Edinburgh was alarmed lest the pestilence should burst forth out of its long sealed-up tomb therein, and work as great havoc as it had done nearly two centuries previously; many people, indeed, left the city, and re- turned not thereto until time had dissipated their fears; but now to return to our tale.

* ' * We have described the day, as being sunny and almost summery; but, as night drew on, the wind suddenly veered round from south to north, and in the month of January that implies a great deal in such a high latitude as Edinburgh. Consequently the heavens were clouded over, and thick flakes of snow had begun to fall, when, close upon midnight, Ivor oh. phant, wearing a long loose cloak, and carrying a bag, which held, for the present, nothing but a well-greased saw and a dark lantern, clambered over a low wall in the rear of the old house in Beth's Wynd, and came to a halt in front of a boarded-over window. He had encountered very few people on the way, for Christmas Eve is not the period of rejoicing, and too frequently of drunken- ness, that it is in England; whilst, once arrived at his destination, our hero had little fear of his labours being interrupted, know- as he did, that no one would approach that supposedly accursed old mansion after nightfall for any consideration whatever. So he laid his bag down amongst the rank weeds and the dead nettles which entirely hid the pavement of the narrow, walled-in courtyard from view, and taking out his saw, set zealously to work upon the black, tarred boards which covered the window through which he had resolved to effect an entrance.

The labour was comparatively easy, so decayed and worm-eaten was the wood, and when the clock of St. Giles's Cathedral began to boom forth the midnight hour, he had made a square orifice amply large enough to admit of his clambering therethrough. Breaking a -pane of glass in the window, he inserted his hand, forced back the catch, and then, though not. without considerable difficulty, and the putting forth of all hi* strength; succeeded in raising the lowei sash. .

A minute later he stood within "Death'f Prison," and as he alighted on the floor, so dense a cloud a dust arose therefrom, that it nearly choked him; whilst, at the shuu? instant, a hundred fiery eye gleamed upon him out of the darkness, and then vanished, as the rats, their owners, with shrill squealt of alarm, darted into their holes. _ _
As quickly as possible Ivor now lighted the candle in his dark lantern, and by its aid looked about him.

The room he had entered was furnished, and on the table stood the remnants of the last meal that had ever been partaken of therein.; but the plates, dishes and glasses, were covered with dust and the air was full of moths. _ _

Believing that the goal of his labours lay- further and higher, Ivor Oliphant opened a door and then ascended a staircase that was full of treacherous holes, but those the light of his lantern enabled him to safely avoid.

The room which he next entered, at the to thereof, proved to be the room, and even our hero's iron will was powerless to prevent him from rushing out of it far more quickly than he had gone in, for there, in a bed, whose counterpane had grown yellow from age, was alcorpse ; and stretched out on the floor yet another, the latter lying on its face with arms and legs stretched out in the shape of a St. Andrew's Cross,andeachhand grasping a bag, whilst stirred by the draught that came up the staircase and th,rough the open door from the broken window, the voluminous black cloak in which the body was draped, fluttered as though he that it covered was still embued with life. _ _ _

—...— The face of the corpse in the bed, with the parchment-hued, dust-covered, moth- perforated clothes tucked up under its chin, was that of a mere skeleton; but stray locks of grey hair, and a long grey beard still adhered to the bare bones. The countenance of the other dead man could not be seen, because it was buried in the carpet. It doubtless, however, pertained to the robber, who, a hundred and three years previously, had posed as Death rendered incarnate, and, thus insolently mocking the dread King of Terrors, had been struck down by him in the midst of ‘is sins in this awful manner; for, all routia him, as he lay there, crucified, as it were, to the floor, was the metallic gleam of gold, and the yet be ht gems and jewels. it entered the room a n of short duration—it struck him that the robber must srAcigoshd tlevrtio srpea—°rkilifmoPer his panic was only have collected all the treasure together, which had been entrusted by his dying patients to Doctor Davie Duncan for safe keeping, before discovering that he had been followed to the house, and firmly secured therein.

Then most probably followed a lingering death from famine, unless, indeed., the Plague had seized upon and consigned him to a quicker, though, more agonising doom. In either case his lust of gold had appa- rently caused him, eventually, to return to that chamber, .so awfully tenanted, and die wallowing in, and greedily clutching at the glittering bait which had lured him on and on, to his destruction, no matter what pre- vious efforts he might have Made to elect his escape. This conviction caused Oliphant to reflect with .a shudder :—what if he had been seen to enter the old house (for he was well aware that many windows commanded a view of its rear as well as of its front), and the terrified neighbours had hurriedly dressed, run out of their homes, and were now -secur- ing him therein, just as that other poor wretch had been secured, more than a century ago; why, then, in another • hundred years (it might be less or it might be more), another searcher after the treasure might he tempted to break into the old house even as he had. and woitld find three dead bodies in that room instuad _of two.
_ In deadly fear that such an event might really be happening, he rushed forward, blae,l; bag in hand, to secure the tempting treasure.

lie fastened his hold, first of all, upon one of the bags of gold which was grasped by a skeleton hand ; but, as he did so, • a shriek smote upon his ears, and he let it 0 twain with a cry that was just as eerie and shrill. "Could the treasure really 'be ghost- guarded,' " he shudderingly wondered ; hut at the same instant the shriek was repeated, and then he knew that it was hut the wind blowing in at the open window downstairs; so he set to work with a bolder heart, cram- ming the gold enclosed in the linen bags, and the hundreds of loose gold pieces, as well as the jewellery which everywhere strewed the dusty, rat-gnawed, moth-perforated carpet, lino his own stout leather bag; and, what was left over, into his every pocket. Then, his task accomplished, be staggered nut of the room; for by that time the close. mephitic air of the chamber of death had well-nigh overcome him, and, after almost reeling down the crazy and dilapidated staircase, gained the window by which he had entered the ancient house half-an-hour previously. It did not take him long to clamber through it, and glad enough he was to breathe once more the pure, fresh, outdoor air.

very. Close Observer would be able to discovii that the wooden barricade ,had eve' been tampered with. Then he clambered over the court-yard wall again, finding it not so easy a feat this time, so heavily was be laden with spoil and, a quarter of an hour later, he had gained his lodgings in Baxter's Close oil the Lawnmarket, where he spent the i etiioind,3l of the night in examining his question., I,ly acquired riches, which ended in the ditcovaq y that he was wealthy beyond even his wituezi hones.
CHAPTER 111.
THE WOFUL WEDDING IN TIIE CHITITCII OF
THE GREY FRIARS.

IVOR OLIPHANT has become, by one bold coup, a rich man. The jewels of at least a score of once leading Edinburgh families, cut off, root and branch, by the Plague, a hundred and three years ago, are now his, and for days he is busy picking out ths stones and melting down the gold settings. One ring!, however, composed of the most lustrous diamonds, he thinks will exactly suit the wedding finger of the lovely girl whom he knows he has securely won, and he keeps it to place over the plain gold hoop that will mark his right of possession ovez her on the performance of the nuptial cere- monies in the old Grey Friar's Church, on the morning of the 24th March; for, as he had gained his fortune on Christmas Day, he had resolved that he would win his wife on Yew Year's Day; and, that he should so 'win her, Muriel Drummond's mercenary father was now well content, for he looked not so much to the man as to the dowry which he would be able to settle upon his daughter, wherefore, so soon as our hero had been able to satisfy him that he was far richer than Sir Ralph Restalrigg, Sir John Drummond gave that ancient swain a sum- mary dismissal, Muriel also breaking her once reluctantly given promise to marry him without so much as the faintest qualm of _conscience.

So Ivor took and furnished a fine house in the, at that time, most fashionable part of Edinburgh, for his bride who was to be, and New Year's Day (which then fell upon the day before Lady Day), at last came round, and with it, at all events to the parties chiefly concerned, the fondly and longingly anticipated wedding. As the bridal cortege entered the gloomy old churchyard on foot, from Candlernaker Row, by way of the steep flight of steps just to the right of the "Martyrs' Monument," bride and bridegroom walking arm in arm, with three fiddlers playing a merry tune immediately in. front of them, and the rest of the wedding party following two and two behind, the lovely Muriel shuddered, and when her lover anxiously inquired the reason, she responded, with an evidently forced laugh: Indeed I cannot tell. Per; haps because someone is walking over the spot where my grave will be," her answer being prompted by a superstition which is not, yet entirely exploded., though the bitter March wind would have been a far more reasonable excuse. _

A minute later, her wandering gaze happening to alight on a high, weed-grown mound that rose bordering the long, straight path which led up to the church porch, and which they were slowly traversing, she asked, in a low tone, "Is not that the spot where those who died of the Plague were buried?" "One of the many spots, my darling; but let not you or I speak ill of the Plague, for has it not given us unto each other?" Ivor Oliphant whispered back; but started and shuddered, in turn, as the last word quitted his lips, for he could have sworn that he heard a hollow voice respond, apparently issuing from underneath the ground, "Mock not at the Plague, for it is about to rend you two apart for ever V" And riow the grey old church is entered, the minister is awaiting them, the service is quickly commenced, and carried on until it reaches the point where the bridegroom has to place the ring upon the bride's finger. He does so, and then he slips over it the flashing diamond one which he has so fondly dedicated to be its guard and keeper. Muriel gives a little gasp of pain as he does so, for something in the ring has pricked her. (It is the tiniest particle of human bone, on the inner side, that has become fixed in the setting, and which Oliphant, often as he had examined it, has never perceived). The next instant, how- ever, the bride is lost in admiration of the beauty of the gems, and the momentary pain is entirely forgotten. The service is soon over, and the wedding party adjourns to the vestry in order to sign the necessary books and registers. Smiling congratulations are passed around. The minister hands Muriel her marriage certifi- cate and Ivor Oliphant gives her a kiss, murmuring the while, in a low tone "Mine, mine for ever." - -
Then he suddenly notices how deathly pale she is, and that some strange-looking black spots have appeared upon her face and hands.

He says nothing to alarm her, but begins to feel terribly though vaguely uneasy, and is thankful when they are outside the church and on their way home. Alas that home, the home which he has been at such joyful pains to prepare for his lovely bride, is destined never to be reached; for half-way down lne long, straight, grave- Yard-path, Muriel's arm slides out of the embrace of his; kind, 'ere he can save her, with, a low, gasping moan, she reels and falls rightacross the rank,weed-grown mound which covers the long-ago buried of the Plague. With a cry of consternation Ivor Oliphant springs forward to lift her up, but . recoils, perfectly appalled by the sudden change in her appearance. The black spots upon her face, which he i had noticed n the vestry, have already doubled in size, and are bubbling, as it were, with corruption. "Keep away from me, lam dying! Oh, I i know that I am dying, and it s from the plague—the plague !" she feebly moans. All fled at the dreadful words; of friends and relatives not one remained behind, save the heart-broken bridegroom and the dis- tracted father.
Poor Muriel, her suffering, though agonis- ing, was brief. She never spoke again, and in ten minutes all was over.

Then Sir John DruMitio-ria would fain have had the poor corpse carried to his house in the Canongate, but by that time the City authorities had appeared upon the scene, and for the safety of the general community aternly forbade such a measure, but insisted upon the body being interred there and then, and their harsh fiat was duly carried out. So Muriel Drummond was wedded and buried in the same hour, nor were father or husband allowed so much as to touch her remains ere she was hidden from their view for ever.._ ,
They themselves were straightway re- moved to the Tolboofh, and kept close prisoners therein no til it became absolutely certain that they had not contracted the fell disease. . .

When they were set at liberty, the flrsi thing that Ivor Oliphant did was to give all his recently acquired wealth to public charities, after which he enlisted in a High. land regiment, just ordered on foreign ser vice, and a year later, he fell, leading a for torn hone, at the capture of rcot. END.
