CHRISTMAS AMUSEMENTS IN THE HOME.
By LUCIE HEATON ARMSTRONG.

Children come home for the Christmas holidays full of vague anticipations of delight, and they sometimes find the time hang a little heavily during the intervals between the various juvenile dissipations which are prepared for them. The house is full of good things, and mother spends half her time at the Stores, ordering more and more goodies and presents, and the children get impatient for the approach of Christ- mas Day, when all the little mysteries will be revealed. Mother gets anxious as she sees the troublesome stage setting in—the bored look of the enfant blase which precedes the terrible query of "What shall Ido now ? " She knows that though she proposes a string of occupations each will be discarded for some good and sufficient reason, and that her letter-writing will be interrupted every minute by the cry of "I'm tired of playing at soldiers, mother," or "What had I better do next ? " Poor mother has a hundred things to do, and she has little time to spare for her children's amuse- ment. How welcome is the loving aunt or the kind elder sister who rises briskly and says: "Let's all play games." The little faces clear up, smiles and good-temper prevail, the game is set going, and one after the other of the family is ensnared in its meshes. A very simple game will please a child. What he really values is the time and attention which his elders give up to him, and the pleasant feeling that they are all doing something together. He is on an equality with them for the time being —nay, their superior, if he is better at games than they are. The leader of the games must be endowed with tact and spirit—spirit to propose a game, and to see that it catches on, and tact to drop it if it is a failure, or before it has gone round too often. Very complicated games are not suitable for children; a game which demands a long explanation is never likely to be a success. The games which I have found most successful in my own family circle are all so extremely simple that I doubt very much if they are worthy the dignity of print; but, nevertheless, I will give a few of them, in case they may be useful to people who are trying to solve the troublesome query of "What shall we play at next ? " Personally I must confess for a preference for GAMES WITHOUT AEPARATUS,

games which can require no hunting for cards, or preparation of any kind, but can be begun in a minute—an instantaneous cure for any little temper or tears which might happen to be on the way. I like these games because they can be played indoors or out of doors, and at any moment; they often wile away a dull moment for a child, or distract its attention when it is unhappy. One of these games is the "Parson's Cat." It is played like this. The first player says: "The parson's cat is an amiable cat." The next one says the same words, only substituting another epithet beginning with A. Not a second must elapse between the speakers, and a forfeit is given to the person who gets to the end of the A's and is forced to begin upon B. "I love my love with an is another game of the same kind, and can always be made amusing if you first calculate the letters so that someone will get the initial of their sweetheart's name.

A game called "Sausages" is sometimes amusing for a couple of rounds when one is playing with very small children. All sit round in a circle, with the exception of the person who asks questions. Three questions are asked of each player in turn, and "Sausages" must be the invariable reply. No laughter! A forfeit is given for the smallest giggle. You must. not laugh, even when you have made out you breakfasted, lunched and dined off these succulent dainties, and that you would prefer them beyond everything else for Christmas presents. "Coffee-pot" is another game of this kind, and it is a great favourite with the little ones. One player goes out of the room, and the others settle on a word for him to guess. He is to ask a ques- tion of each in turn, three rounds being allowed him in which to find out the word. "Coffee-pot" is only the symbol for this word, and it must be introduced into every answer in the place where the right word ought to be. A word with two or more meanings should be chosen, such as bed, box, or ring. Supposing that bed is the selected word, that does for an article of furniture or a flower-bed. Perhaps the questioner begins thus: "Are you tired of playing this game, Teddie ? " Teddie replies: "I am. I would much rather be tucked up in my little coffee-pot." "What is your favourite amuse- ment, Mary ? " asks the questioner, after a pause ig which he has been trying to unravel the meaning cif this oracular reply. "DIGGING IN IfY COFFEE-POT"

is the answer (a garden-bed being implied this time) or "Coffee - potting out my flowers" (bedding-out my flowers). The player through whom the word is discovered has to go out next. time. "Twenty Questions" is a game which "lasts" very well, and it is an excellent exercise for the mind. With very young children I have always found it best to let them think of something in the room. With older people there need be no limit of this kind. One person thinks of something, and the rest of the company have to find out what it is. He is asked a question by each in turn, "yes" or "no" being the only allowable reply. At large parties this game is played with a difference. Two people go out—a lady and a gentleman (and let me remark, in this connection, that many a budding flirtation may be forwarded by a judicious selection of the partners). Two people go out, and two little "clubs "are formed—that is to say, the party splits up into two circles, the chairs being arranged in two rings. Each circle chooses a word. The lady and gentleman return, and one goes into the centre of each group and asks the twenty questions with all possible speed. If the questioner is baffled he has to sit down with the club which has been too clever for him. The club which is the largest in the end is the winning side. "Adjectives" is an amusing- game, at which people of all ages can play. One player goes out, the rest sit round in a semi-circle, and each chooses an adjective which he is to act when the questioner comes in. He must not mention its name. He must convey its meaning through the way in which he answers the questioner. Three questions are allowed for each person. The questioner approaches the first player, who promptly bursts into tears. "What is the matter with you? "he asks. "Oh, nothing!" replies the other with increased sobs. . "Are you mad?" "No." "Silly?" "No." _

u—• " miserable, then? "—as a last resou'rce. "That's it, that's it " with cheerful nods and smiles that the word has been guessed so soon. "Sulky," "affected," "msthetic,' and "joyful," are all good words to choose. "Silly " is rather a nice one, but "mad" give i the greatest scope for dramatic tacent. "New Novels" is a form of Dumb Crambo, the titles of new books being chosen for representation. No speaking is allowed. Everything must be done in dumb show. Two of the party go out, and come in dressed up in some peculiar way, and making certain actions, so as to represent the title of some popular books. "The Heavenly Twins" may be represented by two people of equal height, dressed exactly alike, with nimbuses on their heacts ; or "Peg the Rake" may coins in with a garden-rake and a clothes-pcg. "Judge and Jury" is another game which makes a good deal of fun. "Judge" is seated in a large arm-chair at the top of the room, "jury" in two rows of chairs, facing one another. There are twelve jurymen—or women, as the case may be —and

div.head: JUDGE SITS AT THE TOP
div.p: THE JUDGE SITS AT THE TOP

of the two rows, so that he can be heard at once. He addresses a question to anyone be fancies, and this person must spring up rapidly, say "Certainly, my lud," or words to that effect, and then sit down again. When I say words to that effect, I ought to be more precise. He must not sav "Yes," or "No," and he must say "My hid.'" Also, he must rise from his, chair. If any of these precautions are omitted the most dire event ensues—he is made the judge! He has to change places with that functionary, and to remain on the bench until one of the jury makes one of the mistakes already enumerated. It is not at all nice to be judge! You feel that the eyes of Europe are on you to the most alarming extent, and that you are responsible for keeping the fun going. You should use the name of the person you address, bili you can ask any question you like. "Are you tired of this game, Clorinda " "Do you think that dress suits you, Gladys?" and azything else that occurs to you. "Drawinz Games " are very popular with many young people, anct a great deal or amusement may be got out of a few long narrow slips of paper and some pencils. "Heads, Legs and Bodies" is ;ow ot the best of these games. The paper is foyll
in three. Each player draws a - and then doubles down the paper so that the head cannot be seen, and passes it on to his neighbour. Es adds a body to
head

div.head: TRE INVISIBLE 'LEAD,
div.p: TRE INVISIBLE 'LEAD,

and then passes it on to his neighbour, who add* legs to the body he does not see. The results are most curious. The papers are passed on once more and then unfolded, and the drawings look like the figures on the Egyptian tombs. Oh, my poor lady, whom I started in life with such a pretty facet Has she come back to me with the tody of a cat and the rags of a beggar! And this gallant General with cocked hat and plumes! Can it be possible that he is joined to the body of a goose and wears a ballet-girl's skirt ? None of these creations of the pencil carry out the original idea of their inventors; they depart entirely from the principle en which they were planned. When we have had a couple of rounds, of this we may 'try the "Historical Game" next. Each person draws a scene from history (the worse it is done the better), and it is then passed round to each player in tarn, who writes underneath the title of the picture as it occurs to him, doubling it up so that the next neighbour may not see what he hats written. Sometimes any ordinary object is chosen for a puzzle-picture (without reference to history), and each member of the circle writes what he imagines is the title of it in turn. The results aro often most comic, and the surprise of the artists is often very amusing when they see how their efforts are misconstrued by an inappreciative world. It is often very difficult to distinguish between a cat and a lion, or a fancy portrait and a plum- pudding. I remember one drawing which ran the gamut of a whole family party, being successively labelled by them as a penwiper, a garden-bed with a weed in it, a coal-scuttle, an inkstand with a quill pen sticking upright in it, and how it baffled everyone till it came to the owner of the strange object which the artist had so faithfully endeavoured to depict, who instantly recognised it, and wrote down with gay confidence "My bonnet "! Her bonnet it was—that dainty confection of velvet with its single upstanding plume which had been the standing joke of her family ever since she had bought it; and shouts of laughter greeted the caricature as everyone had a look at it the second time. This is not a game that can be played many times running, and the same thing applies to "Consequences," which is always an amusing game.

div.head: Foßrurs.
div.p: Foßrurs.

At Christmas-time many children's games have forfeits, and I think this is one of the most difficult parts of the evening's entertainment. The "forfeit.. holder" has always to call his or her ingenuity to work to find some fresh penalty for the victim to. pay. Here are fifteen forfeits which I think will help my readers this festive time :
1: Put yourself through the keyhole. This is done by writing the word "yourself " a small piece of paper and passing it through tho keyhole. ••
2. Kiss a book inside and out without opening it. This is done by kissing a closed book in the room, then opening the door and kissing the book, outside the room.
3. Sing in one corner, dance in another, whistle in another, and cry in another. 4. Stand on a chair, and wait till one of the opposite sex comes and kisses you and lifts you down.
5. To be blindfolded, and kissed by one of the opposite sex, and to guess who it is.
6. Lie down on the floor, and get up on your feet without touching the ground with your elbovra or hands.

7. If a gentleman, put a chair on its side and hop over it; if a lady, put a foot-stool on the top of another and hop over it. 8. Call your sweetheart's name up the chimney. 9. Bite an inch off the poker. This is done by biting something an inch away from the poker. "

10. Look in a looking-glass, and all the people of the opposite sex pass behind you and look over your shoulder. You frown on all those except the one you like best, and you smile on that one. 11. Say the alphabet backwards quickly. 1.2. Count up to one hundred, saying the word "Buzz" when a number containing a seven, or s multiple of that number, occurs. 13. Light a candle, blindfold the victim, turn him round three times, and then let him walk up to the candle and blow it out. Each time he fails he must pay another forfeit. 14. Take off your shoes, put two chairs together, and jump over them. This is done by taking off your shoes, putting two chairs together, and jumping over your sitor.' not the chairs.
15. Dow to the wittiest, kneel to the prettiest, and kiss the one you love best.

div.head: DECEMBER 23rd, 1898.
div.p: DECEMBER 23rd, 1898.

Somn change is evident in The Change in the the form of the CzA.n.' Czar's Prpposal. proposal, according to the latest news from St. Petersburg. It was too com- prehensive before, and it is now to be somewhat restricted. It will not, apparently, be made to include a consideration of the relative position of the European Powers and of questions likely to have any permanent effect on the peace. We take it that Alsace-Lorraine is not to. be mentioned nor the condition of European Turkey. It almost looks as if the proposed suggestion of arbitration was to be ab led° lel As now stated it is to be restricted to the question of armaments, and the best way of preventing costly competi- tions in this direction. The new idea is that the Ambassadors of the various Powers at St. Petersburg shall meet together, after they have been duly instructed by their respective Governments, under the presidency of Count IVlcnevrEFF. Their Lusiness will be to discuss the general idea, and to frame some recommenda- tions, if possible, upon which a series of practical conclusions can be based, to be drawn out by specialists. Tito "Times" correspondent at St. Petersburg views the programme as" a simple one, as compared with the expectations to which the MIIRAVIEFF circular of last August at first gave rise." The new proposal has yet to be put into an official form, and this cannot be done until the CZAR returns from Livadia, which will be in about a fortnight's time. The change will not be regarded, in some quarters, as wholly if or the better. If arbitration is to be knocked out of the programme there will be much less romance in it for the new crusaders in favour of peace. The various Governments have approved of the dis- cussion which was originally proposed by the CZAR'S rescript. But they have contented them- selves with welcoming a generous idea. They will now have to deal with the subject of specific measures, and there may not be quite the same unanimity. At first the notion was that an Ambassador would have been specially designed for a congress in some neutral city, to represent each Power, and to enter upon and settle the whole matter if possible. The Conference of Ambassadors who will have to be briefed by their respective Governments is a businesslike proposi- tion, but it will have to be rigidly kept to the matter in hand. If the conference should be unable to agree as to the feasibility of reducing armaments, or maintaining the status quo, the whole scheme will drop. If they should agree, the matter may go forward, and a good deal of time will necessarily be taken up in hearing experts from the different countries. Whether these experts can make real propositions without betray- ing national plans is one of the points of consider- s* moment which must enter into the general examination of the conference which must be taken by each Power before instructing its Ambassador. The change hardly seems, in our judgment, to make the success of the project more certain. It is obviously the result of the international discus- sions which have taken place, and these discus- sions will now have to be actively resumed.

TEM attempt to make one ( Trade and Strikes, class of the community re- sponsible for some of the diversions of trade which are going on is mani- Wetly unfair. If a machinist receives orders to make machinery to go abroad, which is intended to produce abroad that which we have hitherto manufactured at home, it would be obviously un- just to blame his workmen for diverting domestic trade. The process has been going on for many years in various branches of industry, and the re- sults are to be seen in the making of many varie- ties of goods in nearly every country of the Con- tinent. It is legitimate trade, men say, and no blame can be attached to either party. But the moment two parties to a dispute about wages which occurs are in opposition the blame is in- stantly heaped on the wage-earners. They are told that they should be content with low wages in the general interests of British trade. The matter is one of which they must judge for them- selves. On the other hand, if masters regard it as more important that their profits should never fall below a certain point than that they should run the risk of foreigners getting their orders,they are, economically,in just the same position as their men. They are subordinating national to private interests. The duty of the nation in such cases seems to us to be clear. It must provide for the protection of its general interests by making these disputes as short as possible. The Engineering dispute, which has indirectly resulted in some orders going abroad, and the Welsh .coal dispute, which increased the demand. for Japanese and Vir- ginian coal, caused a real loss to the country. Could the State have interposed and adjusted these troubles at once, some thousands of pounds would have been saved to the country, to say nothing of privation and suffering to persons not directly con- cerned. We hold, in fact, that for any loss of trade which a huge and prolonged trade war causes to the country, master, men, and Parliament are alike to blame. If our trade is of real value, if British interests are the true concern of the Government, if public opinion is ever to have ethical and binding force, we must seek real remedies for real evils. Retaining trade, with the risk of impoverishing workmen and throwing more strain on the poor law, is not a wise policy in national interests. But it was a Wise policy to utilise the results of experience. Demands and resistance are prejudicial if long mtinued. We can prevent this continuance by

legal enactments, and we osght not tY;hasitate much longer. If, say, a judicial tribunal la IdEd e- cided against the men in the engineering and:coed wars, and they had accepted the decision and re- sumed work, it would clearly have been a general gain. Persons who admit this mast a knit th e converse, though they seldom have the logic to do so. That is the weak point of the whole affair. It is always assumed that the men are wrong and ought to give way. Assume that masters can sometimes be wrong, and judicially arbitrate be- tween- them, and the advance will be good all round.

Few public men have had such a marvellou gift of clear, incisive speech, and have been so thoroughly mismiderstood,as Mr. Justice Hawkins. His reputation as a martinet has been gained in his defence of prisoners from the Bench,frequently in saving them from their own counsel. A per- fect balance of mind is beyond humanity, but the leaning of the octogenarian judge who is now re- tiring has been for the prisoner and against the prosecution as to the admission of evidence. It is unnecessary to recall his thousand and one rebukes to pushfal police-officers in support of this view. That a prisoner who was found guilty had nothing to hope for in any way of lenity at his hands is within common knowledge ; but the extent of the punishment, subject as it is to revision by the public through the Home Secretary, is a small ;natter compared with the determination of the issue of guilt or innocence. Sir Henry Hawkins quite early in his judicial career made one blunder by which a woman afterwards believed to be innocent,was very nearly hanged. That was in the Staunton trial, when his directions to the jury induced them to include in their verdict of guilty Alice Rhodes, the com- panion of Lewis Staunton. The Home Secretary corrected the error by a free pardon, and since that time it may be said that the safest judge to try a capital offence has been Sir Henry Hawkins. lie has always borne in upon a jury that no blem- ish of character of an accused person should in- fluence thorn in their conclusions upon the imme- diate facts. It is easy to understand how differ- ent would have been his se aiming up in the Work trial to that of Mr. Justice Pffillimore,about which even the staidest law journals cannot keep silent. It is equally certain thatoinlike Mr. Justice Ridley, he would not have told a prisoner before he went into the witness-box that his story was improb- able, and so have discounted it in the eyes of the jury. ft was as a stickler for precision that Mr. Justice Hawkins got his name for austerity; but the austerity was in the interest of the weak.

The ion. Sterling Morton, Secretary for Agri- culture under President Cleveland, is heading a crusade against Christmas trees which promises to develop° into a powerful movement across the water, as it has at its back statesmen and writers and landowners who understand the value of affore- station, and are prepared to make the issue a political one. Tie objectors to the ancient cus- tom are not only powerful in themselves, but they have on their side an encouraging show of reason. The official statistics show that last year in the States more than twenty million Christmas trees were cut down and put on the market, and the immense denudation t,f woodlands is more than ' the annual planting of all kinds of trees. Thus there is constant decrease in the area of forest land, isolated copses are disappearing, and the question has become of national importance. As Mr. Morton remarks, the absurdity of celebrating the Birth of the Founder of Christianity by a wanton waste and extravagance which jeopardises the welfare of millions of human beings yet un- born is obvious, and must within a very few years be regarded as intolerable by those whose duty it is to preserve the possessions of the nation and hand them down intact to the proper inheritors. We do not pretend to know how affairs stand in England, but in view of the deplorable neglect of affoiestation here, and the danger it involves, it would be useful to have some official statistics, and to seek to apply the lesson they teach, as the Americans intend t I do.

The Prince of Wales's powerful advocacy of the crusade against consumption should do much to make it efficacious. The medical men can do no- thing without the co-operation of the public,who, so long as they coo in health, maintain a curious scepticism as to the possibility of their catching disease, and consequently never trouble to take precautions. A large section, however, has a loyal regard for the opinions of Royalty,and it is to this section that the Heir Apparent's advocacy will appeal. The ffational Association for the Preven- tion of Csnsumption which was launched this week at Marlborough House, recognises the stupend- ous nature of the task it has undertaken. The in- siciious disease is increasing. Milk and meat as- sist its growth, owing to improper or inefficient examination. It is in the dust of the atmosphere, but can usually be avoided thereby using the com- monsense precaution provided by nature—breath- ing through the nostrils only. The association has very properly announced its intention of educat- ing the people in prophylactics, while at the same time making provision for those who have the good sense when the malady is incipient to take active steps for its suppression. Sanatoria in Eng- land, where patients can live at front 15s to 30s a week, should reduce the scourge to half its present I dimensions—always given the sensible co-opera- tion of the general public.

Mr. Justice Mathew has brought himself into unusual prominence by his expression of opinion anent the use of the " cat " upon a certain class of criminals. His opinion moreover has come in for severe, and pretty general condemnation. The worthy Judge disapproves of the lash as a punish- ment for offences against women and children, ad- vancing as his reason the sentimental argument that men guilty of these abominable crimes have, in many instances, previously borne good charac- ters and finally succumbed tosudden temptation. We are willing to bow to the experience of Mr. Justice Mathew in this particular—probably the men have had a mere or less satisfactory moral character sometime or other—but we entirely dis- sent from his contention that they should escape the dreaded " cat "on that account. Individuals with the best of characters occasionally commit the crime of murder, but they are hanged for their offence all the same, and wo see no reason what- ever why they should not be forced to endure the corporal punishment so feared if they are guilty of criminal assault on a weak member of the op- posite sex,and which in some respects is even worse than murder. Crimes of this description are far too common in this country—there has been an awful instance at St. Helens recently—and deterrent measures of too severe a character cannot be used. Public opinion, as evidenced by the frequent re- commendations of grand juries, is in favour of the "cat" being utilised to put a stop to such offences. Garroting was chocked by similar means, and to hesitate now about inflicting the lash on brutes of a lower type is nothing less than false humanitar- ianism, and dangerous to the public safety.

TRAP FATALITY AT WIDNES.

On Tuesday -O;4N- rsry Wainrbt labaurer em- ployed by Mr. Bate, Warrington-road, Raiahill, was driving a horse and trap along Willmere-lane Widnes, to the Black Horse Inn,Farnworth,and when near to Loot's Heath-road, in some unalcauntable manner the trap. received a sudden jerk and Wainwright was pitched out When picked up he was found to be lifeless, On Thurs- day an inquest was held and a verdict of acedontal death returned.

RUNCORN TECHNICAL INsrirurx. In connection with the Art classes at the above In- stitute, a students' sketching club has been formed. Mr. M. L. Davies is president, and Mr. J. F. Beck acts as secretary, The Committee consists of Misses Wiswall and Tatters, and Messrs. T. Clare and W. T. Howard. The objects of the club are to stimulate original work among the students, and to provide exercise in art apart from the instruction received at the classes. The club is entirely controlled by the students, and will no doubt be of great benefit to them, and also to the Institute.e

DEATH OF AN OLD RIINCORNIAN.I There passed away on Tuesday at his residence trractc- ley-street, in th 3 person of Mr. James Gregory, aged 79 years, a familiar figure that will be sadly missed. Born at Padgate, near WaLrington, Mr. Gregory came to Run- corn, many years ago, and up to about 20 years ago was employed as sawyer at Messrs. Brundritt and Co.'s shipyard. For years he filled the post of absentee visitor at the Brunswick Sunday school, and as instan- cing his deep attaehment to Methodism, it is interesting to note the remarkable way in which during his life Mr. Gregory could recall texts and parts of sermons de- livered by such great preachers as Dr. Beaumont and Dr. Newton, both of whom he had heard. He also possessed a phenomenal know- ledge of the Wesleyan Hymn Book and could quote it from cover to cover. And his knowledge of " Alphabetical Arrangement" was truly remarkable. Of late years he was a frequent visitor at the Free Library and being a gentleman of means did many kind acts in an unostentatious manner.

PHILHARMONIC SOCIETY'S SOCIAL AND DA.NCE. Inder the auspices of the Runcorn Philharmonic Society a most successful social and dance was held at the Drill Hall on Wednesday night.—Mr. T. Knight's band played for dancing which was spiritedly kept up until about two o'clock the following morning. Mr. George Pearson was the efficient " M.C." During the social the refreshment tables were presided over by : Misses Simkin, Crosby, Taylor, and Withington. On the whole a most enjoyable evening was spent. Sr. PAUL'S P.S.E. WIDNES. The animal was a valuable one, and was only purchased a fe years ago for 30 guineas.

THIS CHRISTMAS SHOW. In accordance with the annual practice of the town and district the "Christmas Show" WAS held on Thurs- day evening. Shops were got up in the most attractive style, and the devices resorted to for the purpose of en- tertaining the crowds that visited tha various streets, and for riveting their attention were ingenious. Tile streets were fitted win a large crowd up to a late hour, and if evidences of Christmas's approach wete wanting in any way it was only the mildness of the weather prevailing, that was at fault. It is intereiting to learn that the Christmas philanthropist with his seasonable gifts is not unknown in Runcorn, and that our poorer neighbours are not entirely noolected during this season of "goodwill cowards all men." RUNCORN AND WIDNES CO-OPERATIVE EMPLOYES TONTINE SOCIETY. The annual meeting of the above Society was held on Tuesday night, Mr. J. J. S taw presiding. It was with deep regret that the Society recorded the death of its lae s.cretary, Mr. Walter Lacey, and a high tribute was pail to his worth during his official connection with

the Seciety. The annual s-tatement and balance sheet. was submitted by the treasurer, Mr. C. H. Johnsoae and it showed an expenditure of £lO6 is 43,--,d; receipts, £lOB 123 8d; balance £2 5s 31. The auditors were Messrs. James Haynes 'and Arthur Patin. The othsr officers :,—J. L. Withington (secretary), T. Clare, Run- corn Steward ; and G. Cann,Widnes steward ; were also present, and the whole werere-alected. INQUEST AT RUNCORN. At the Rune ern Police Court, on Saturday morning, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body of Mrs. Eliza Ceok, 59, Surrey-street, who was found deal in bad on Thursday morning, last week.—Miss Edith Cook, said the deceased was her mother, and the widow of the late Mr. William Cook. She was 59 years of age. Deceased had complained of pains in the stomach, and appeared exhausted after undue exertion. On waking at about 6.15 on the Thursday morning, wit- ness found that her mother was dead.—Dr. McLennan, Runcorn, stated that he had attended the deceased during her lifetime, for indigestion. Since death he had seen the body and considered the cause of death to be sudden failure of the heart's action.—The jury brought in a verdict of " Death fc,An natural causes," and a vote of condolence with the bereaved children was subse- quently passed by them. Oa Monday afternoon a large and representative gathering of the leading gentlemen of Widnes met at Ditton-road Chambers, Widne' s for the purpose of pre- senting to the Mayor of the borough, Alderman J. N. Wareing, his portrait, paintql by Mr. JIMPg 1119/aster, as a token of the esteem in which he is held be fluffier- one friends in tke town. The portrait was on view at the recent art exhibition, and was greale admired as a true reprevatation of his Worship in his rohes of office. The proceedings were prasid?d over by Mr. J. Hirst, and the presentation was m,cle be Major R. Lewis, who re- ferred Sc.his long acquaintance and intimate friendship with Alderman Major Wareing, as a friend, neighbour, volunteer, busimrs man, and magistrate.—Messrs. J. Morrison, Councillor G. I. Niel, B. Brown, F Niel, C.C., and Councillor T. Carney,also supported the testimonial. —The Mayor, in respending, said he was simply over- whelmed by their kindness, and he could only say that his one object in life had been to live in harmony with his fellow men and that whatever he was called upon to perform to do it in the most conscientious manner be possibly could. He thanked them from the bettem of his heart, and said he would Sr.'s sure the gift as one of his most precious possessions. (Applause.) S. RUNCORN PAUPER'S FATS. Mr. S. Brighouse he'd an inquest at the Blackburne Arms, Ditton, on Tubs lay, conc-raing the death of Celia Gibling a single worn in, aged thirty-three, who was found dead on the London and North-Western Railway close to Ditton Junction on Saturday night last, at twenty minutes o eleven. Deceesed was found by Locornotive-inspe .tor Oakley lying in the four-foot of the Runcorn up-tins, with her left hand cut off, and a cut on the temple.—John Marston, induqtrial trainer at Dutton Workhouse of the Runcorn Union, identified the body. and said that deceased ha I been an inmate of that institution off and on since June, 1893. On the 3rd inst she was given into the custody of the Runcorn police for refractory conduct at the Workhouse, and on the sth inst. was sentenced to foarteen days, imprison- ment. She was liberated from Knutsford Gaol on Satur- day last, and a porter at Allerton Station named John Thomas deposed that he saw deceased alight there at four o'clock on Saturday from the Northwich train. Deceased said she had been over-carried, having inten- ded to get off at Runcorn, and elle inquired the time of departure of the next train for that place. He directed her to the train and deceased was last seen at five o'clock on Ditton Junction Station platform. Where she had to change for Runcorn, crossing the end of the line to reach her train on No.l platform. No evidence was forthcoming as to her subsequent movements, and the jury returned an open verdict.

On Wednesday night the annual meeting of the Bruns- ' wick Mutual Improvement Class was held at the Bruns- wick Schoolroom. Mr T Simister presided, and there was a good attendance of members. After a resume of the work of the session had been given the election of officers was proceeded with :—Mr T Simister was re-elected president, on the motion of Mr W Mill.ngton seconded by Mr Lawton.—The other officers elected were vice- president, Mr J D Jones ; secretary, Mr J J Pickthall ; committee, Misses Crosby, Baker, Hayes, Taylor, Mc- Donald, Mrs Pickthdl, Messrs J Douglas, G Hayes, W T Saunders, J D Bisbrown, W Jones, J Sim- kin, and P Unsworth.—Mr A Dodd, OA retiring secre- tary received a hearty vote of thanks fir his past ser- vices which extended over many sessions, after which he evening was spent in a clavivi id manner.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
LBY A CORRESPoNDENT]

A Nonconformist Union is to be formed in Run- corn, having for its object the consolidating and furthering of Nonconformist interests, and already the initiatory steps have been taken. The need of the union is manifest, and will be heartily wel- comed by all members of Nonconformist bodies as a common platform upon wiich to meet and form a common policy so as to present a united front when occasion arises. The regret is that such a union has not before this been in existence, in the district.

At the Runcorn Rural District Council meeting mention was made of the Rivers' Pollution Acts, and a letter from Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk of the County Council, discloses the fact that there exists a considerable amount of sewage that finds its way into the several streams and water courses within the district, and during a desultory discussion the opinion was generally expressed that the County Council were, to say the least, exacting. Whether that is so or not the fact remains that at least there exists a " technical pollution "—it nothing more— and the County Council are bound to take cogniz- ance of it,and indeed some of those "technical" pol- lutions (so-called) are absolutely unknown quanti- ties, in the existence of which there lurks a risk. Therefore the County Council are—if exacting— justly so, in carrying out protective measuros.

The after effects of the School Board election are to be distributed amongst us and will form, per- haps, the chief topic of conversation for Christmas- tide. To say that the whole town is on fire would be to put it mildly. The cause of the latest stir is the " inquest " held at the church schools on Tues- day night. it was a judicious step to take, and showed that the Church Party are determined not to countenance such proceedings as those alleged, on the part of any school teacher, and entitles them to credit for an act of honesty,

about the whole affair; others that there was no Of course, many will say there is an absurdity need at all for such a procedure ; But how about the old adage" Where there's smoke there's fire ?" The evidence is before the public and from it they ought, and I think will, draw their own conclusions. Whatever they be my only,hope is that they may be charitable/ones.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Another win for Runcorn was recorded on day and consequently the club has gained some- thing of its old popularity. Thera was not such a good display of the game as usual on Saturday; but Warder, Farmer, Houghton, Walker and Hailwooi showed no mean form all through.

Hopes of a sustainedimprovement in the club's position in the Senior Competitbn are now gener- ally entertained for J. Butterworth and Faulkner have consented to figure in the team and make their first appearance, on Saturday against Broughton Rangers at Broughton. This is a matter for some congratulation; though I still think the club might have done better had they accepted Warrington's offer of £6O or £7O.

Runcorn team for Saturday, against Broughton Rangers at Broughton: back, S Houghton; three- quarters, D Jones, T Warder, J Butterworth, T Wilkinson; half backs, J Jolley, and J Faulkner; forwards, A Taylor, S Walker, W Lightfoot, Li Farmer, F Gayter, F Darlington, 0 Hughes and It Reece.

The fortnightly mooting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, when there Were present :—Messrs. J. Stokes (presiding). A. R. Norman, 8. Taylor, T. Lea. T. Reynolds, with the members of the Rural District' Council. and Mr. George F. Ashton (deputy clerk). THE LADIES' COMMUTEE. Mr. Stokes intirnat.-d that he had received a letter from Mr. J. Mosley Williams stating h 3 was unable to prevail upon any Frodsharn lady to act in place of Miss He yes (retired). Mr. Mclntyre proposal the election of Mrs. Mosley Leigh, Bel Monte. Mr. Baxter s.:conded and the motion was unanimously agreed to. THE DOCTORS AND THE VACCINATION ARRANGEMENTS. As Chairman of the P tritamentary Committee, Mr. J. Mclntyre, submitted the report of the meeting bold prior to the Beard meeting. It would be remembered that the Beard had fixed upon the minimum fee for the carrying out of the vaccination orders, and that the doe'ors had declined to accep.% The result was that they met that morning and came to a satilfactnv at- ranzemeut. The fees arranze I upon were is. 81. and 53, for cases within a mile of the doct)r's residence, and for distances beyond a mile to the full extent of tao dis- trict an additional half-crown. Mr. A. R. Norman in seconding the resolution to adopt the report said the arrangement was for t we've months, and if necessary there c suld b 3 a revision at the end of that time, The report was Unanimonsly aoopted. CHRISTMAS TREAT FOR THE INMATES. The report of the Ladies' Committee disclosed that the house had been via ted and the wards were found to be in a satisfactory condition. The ladies proposed to give their annual Christmas treat to the inmates of the House I on January 11th 1899. The tea would be followed by an ' entertainment, in the Dining Hall in which meet of the members of the Committee had promised to take part. Miss Dutton (the president) undertook to send invita- tions to the Guardians and to the Chaplain ; and Mrs. Baxter with her usual kindneSs offered the use of her piano. Mr. T. Lea proposed and Mr. E. Clarke seconded a vote of thanks to the Ladles' Cscomittee, which was un- animously carried.

FINANCES. Out relief was granted as under 3—Runcorn, £B5 ; Frodsbam, £24 ; Budworch, £23 ; other payments amounted to £3l 16s 4d. The ba'ance last Board was £2,541 173 81 ; received since, £479 13s 10 ; deducting the total payments (£163 163 43), there was a balance remaining of £2,857 153 21.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION. HANDS UP FOR CHURCH OR CHAPEL P IMPORTANT INQUIRY BY THE SCHOOL MANAGERS.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION. HANDS UP FOR CHURCH OR CHAPEL P IMPORTANT INQUIRY BY THE SCHOOL MANAGERS.

On Tuesday evening the managers of the Runcorn National School held an inquiry,in one of the classrooms of the Girls' School, into an allegation that had been made that a mistress had asked the children in her class to declare whether they belonged to the church or to chapel. The managers present were the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, vicar (in the chair), Rev. H. B. Firth, Messrs. E. Imison, C.C., W. Mellor, J. Johnson, E. New- ton, and H. White. Mr. F. A. Lake represented Miss Woodward, assistant mistress, and Mr. A. T. Davies (H3rbert Lewis and Davies, Liverpool) appeared for Mr. Wesley Cooke. There was a large number of teachers present, several parents, and the Revs. S. Wright, C. W. L. Christian, J. A. B. Malvern, and J. Osborne, and Mr. A. Jordan, headmaster. The Chairman said this enquiry was on behalf of the raanagers of the school into a certain charge which had been made in writing against one of the mistresses teasployed by them in the school. The managers having knowledge that certain charges were flying about from mouth to mouth in the town, first took no notice of them because such things were not uncommon but after a certain letter had been published, and sent he believed to every household in the town, and the managers hav- ing been informed that a certain gentleman had deliber- ately and distinctly made a charge in a public place thought that he should be compelled to substantiate the charge. The solicitor to the managers wrote to this gentleman and the consequence was that the charge was put in writing and that inquiry was held. He called upon Mr. Lake to read the charge as it now stood. 4, Lowlands-read, Runcorn, December 16E6, 1898.

Sir,—Your note of the 14th to hand while substanti- ally correct, contains inaccuracies which I cannot admit. My st APiront is:—Tuat after toe School Board Election, in Miss Siivre school, other wise the National School, otherwise the Parish Church School, children were made to signify by show of hands which belonged to the Church an i which, belonged to the Chapel, and that this distinguishing of the Church children from the Chapel children naturally led to the annoyance of the few Chapel children that were brave esongh to avow their religious convictions under such trying circumstances. Before making this statement I satisfied myself of its accuracy, and your clients know, or. ought to know, that . their Miiitreas (Miss Woodward) and any of the cbildrOn in her charge on the occasion in question can substantiate what I have stated. If you: clients are sin- cere in their assert' .ns " that the statement is absolutely false and without the slighter, shadow of foundation," I can only express my surprise that they should be ignor- ant of what has bsen public property since the chldren were dismissed on the afternoon in question.—l remain, yours etc.,

(Signed) WISLEY C. COOKE. The Chairman said toe managers felt that any charge of injustice to any child in that school was one that would reflect most ssriously, if it were true, upon the school awl one whioh in their judgment would be, if it were proved, of a most serious nature. They felt that if any teacher were guilty of any kind of injustice to- wards any child that she would be acting in a way that would merit Severe condemnation on the part of the managers. Theref ere they wished to investigate this cese thoroughly and openly. Perhaps Mr. Cook as the person who brought the charge would stand up and answer any question which might be put to him. Mr. Davies: I represent Mr. Cook. Toe Cnairman asked whether the written charge which bad just been read was the whole charge that had to b 3 made. The messes they (the managers) wished to know this was that they had information that the charge as originally made in public was different from that which had been put before them in writing. There- fore he asked whethee the charge was the same in writ- ing or a different charge from that made openly in a railway carriage. Mr. Davies said if it were convenient he would state Mr Cooke's position in this matter. He represented Mr. Cooke on very short notice, a very few hours, but they felt the importance of the matter so much that they had responded to the intimation that the managers wOuld hold that public inquiry that day. He felt strongly,how- ever,as expressed in a letter to Mr. Lake on the previous day :—" It is obvious however that an inquiry con- ducted by your own clients, the managers, who have in- etructei you to take legal proceedings against Mr. Cooke. can hardly commend itself to that gentleman or anyone else as a tribunal sufficiently independent to be competent to deal impartially with the case nor will the holding of the inquiry on the school premises tend to im- prove matters.' The Chairman, interrupting, said the question was a simple one—the Managers wished to kaow whether Mr. Cooke was bringing that one charee or any others. Mr. Davies: If you will allow me to proceed with this inquiry I would state exactly the position Mr. Cooke occupied. The Chairman : If Mr. Cooke does not answer that question, the inquiry will be at an end. Mr. Davies said it was desirable that the inquiry should be as summary as possible. Although the notice of the incpeiry had been very short, he was there to proceed distinctly with the charge, sad there might be other things arising out of it. The Ohairman : When they arise it will be time to consider them. Mr. Davies said they did arise, and they hoped for the serious consideration of those', desirous of getting at the truth of the matter. Although his client would have preferred an indepsndent investigation, they were there to render assistance in making a complete inquiry, but it should go to the public that the managers have already prejudged the question by the Statement in a letter by their solicitor that the statement "is absolutely false and without the slightest shadow of foundation." That was why it would have been better to have an in- dependeat tribunal. They coald not be judge and jury in the same cause. The Chairman : Your client has made a distinct charge against one of our employes and our business is to inquire into it. Mr. Davies said he was net there to put any obstacles in the way but to make the inq airy as full as possible but no ordinary person would approve of a tribunal which was not independent and which had already passed judgment upon the thing. The Chairman said the managers were the only tribu- nal that possibly could try the Case. A charge of cruelty or brutality of some kind was brought against one of the teachers and it was the business of the managers te try such a case as that. Mr. Davies : But not to nass judgment upon it first. The Chairman : You had no business to bring teat forward at all. Mr. Davies : You instructed the solicitor to write the letters. After some furth.r conv.raatioh Mr. Davies said the charge was that stated in Mr. Cooke's letter. The Chairman : And nothing else ? Mr. Davies Only subsequent (overate. The Chairman: Answer the question. Mr. Davies : I am not here to be lecture lor bullied. We have formulatod a charge in writing. If toe teachers have done anything since in Gonne tiers with anyone of the scholars that I apprehend must he in- quired into. The Chairman : That is a subsequent charge to this. You don't bring any charge now? Mr. Lake : They hope by a fishine inquiry,they may find something. Mr. Davies said his charge was at present confined to the charge in the letter, but he should not commit him- I self not to inquire no further. M s; Kennion,an assistant mistress in the boys' school, was called and said on the Saturday after the School Bear I Election she was going down to Liverpool and she got into a carriage where there were Mr. Cooke and a lady, and the conversation turned on the election. ' She listened and heard Mr. Cooke say that after' the Election was oiler Miss Sewell, the senior mistress at the National Schools. asked the children which girls went to Chapel. Some girls put their hands up and then the teacher asked which girls went to Church, and some other girls put their hands up. Miss Woodward then said "Now are you not glad that you go to Church ?" Mr. Cooke then said that in the boys' school Mr. Jordan was beard be, say to Ulf, boys not ti take out the white bills but to to take the yellow bills. , The yellow bills are ours. She said to Mr. Cooke " That's a lie." Mr. Cooke asked how did she know it was a lie and she replied, because she was present and could testify th the charge. After this Mr. Cooke talked on other topics. Crns,examined by Mr. Davies : She did not know Mr. Cooke to speak to. As regarded what was said to have taken place in the girl's school she believed the teacher before the children. Miss Sewell, the head mistress, was called and MO pervnally she knew nothing about the church or chapel question. She had not asked for a show of hands, but she had heard the charge against Miss Woodward and she lead made an inquiry amongst the children. She called out those children who had signed those papers about Miss Woodward. She asked why they had signed those papers and the children replied that Mr. Norman and Mr. Christien had got them to sign the papsrs. Three or four children had signed the papers stating that Miss Woodward had asked for a show of hands for the church children and a show of hands for chapel children. , The three or four children on Fridae and on Monday last said Miss Woodward had done se. The other children in the class denied this. The teacher said she had not done so and she believed the teacher before the children in a matter like this. There would be 45 children in the class and only three or four spoke to Miss Woodward asking for a show of hands. Lillie Faulkner in answer to the Chairman said she was now in Standard IV under Miss Woodward. She had been brougnt up in school from the infants' depart- ment. She was nine years of aee. She had been treated kindly. By Mr. Davies : She remembered the day after the election. In the afternoon, daring the poetry lesson,one

gig put her hand up and said the Church had got in. Miss Woodward then asked the children who went to church to put their bands no which they did. She then asked tie girls who went to Chapel to put their hands up which they did. Then a few church girls started laugh- ing at the chapel girls. Witness was oaa who held up her hand for chapel. Then Miss Woodward said "Well, never mind, it doesn't matter where von go to so long as you go to some place. Witness described how Miss Sewell had questioned her on the matter on Friday and Mon- day. Miss Sewell said she was a "deliverer.' (Laughter.) She could not pronounce the word and she did not know what it meaot. Miss Sewell said it was very strange that four girls should remember and the other girls not remember what Miss Woodward had said. Miss Wood- ward had been kind, to her and slse had no grudge against her. By Mr. Lake: She first told her mother what had taken place. Witness repeated exactly the statement she had made to Mr. Davies. It was only a few church children that laughed and Miss Woodward stopped them. She was sure it was Miss Woodward who asked them to Put their hands up. Mr. Norman and Mr. Christien saw her about a fortnight after the election and she told them it was true. She was not hurt in any way nor in- sulted by being asked to hold up her hand for Chapel. She signed the paper, and she repeated what she had told in the paper. Mr. Lake : Do you always know your lessons as well as this ? Mr. Davies : No, no. Mr. Lake : It is too palpably pat: M. Davies: You might make it no more absurd and unofficial than it is.

By the Chairman : She did not write the paper herself Mr. Norman wrote it and asked her to sign it. Mr. Davies said statutory declarations bad been taken before a justice of the peace and witnesses were there and prepared to give evidence. The Chairman : Do you mean thstthis child has made • statutory declaration ? Mr. Davies: Yes.sir. The Chairman : It is wonderful it is not put in. Mr. Davies : lam conducting my case in a proper way by putting in viva tree evidence. Maud Deakin, who had beau brought up in the schnol, since an infant and was now in the fourth standard said Miss Woodward was a very kind teacher. By Mr. Davies: Sae was ten years of again answer to Mr. Davies' guestionslshe made statements corroborative of Lillie Faulk ier. She remembered what had taken place well. adisi Sewell asked her yesterday if she bad no: said chapel was nettelr than church and she replied that she had not said it.

By Mr. Lake: May (best had said that chapel was better than church. Oa the Saturday after the election Mr. Norman came to her and asked her what had taken placs, and she .told him, she did not remember who started talking about the election in the class. Did not Miss Woodward say" Yes the Church has went and the Vicar is at the head of the poll, but we have nothing to do with that; let us get to our poetry ?" —Yes.—Did she say that at once ?—Yes.--Who was it said put your hands up P—Miss Woodward. She was sure it was not some of the children. The children did net." boo "at each other. Miss Woodward said it did not matter whetker they went to church or chapel so long as they did not play in the streets.—You did not feel hurt about it P—No.—You looked upon it as a bit of fun ?—Witoess smiled. . The Chairman: You signed the paper, did you?— Yes.—The same paper that Lillie Faulkner signed ? Mr. Davies: I can relieve you about that. They are separate papet s. Tne Chairman: Who was the magistrate you declared before ? Mr. Davies: It was Mr. Norman. Mr. Lake observed that Mr. Norman had acted in two capacities. Mr. Davies said Mr. Norman was there as a magistrate and Mr. Osborne was with him. Mr. Norman did not act in two capacities. Mr. Lake : lie did evidently. Mr. Davies : Mr. Osborne took the evidence down. Mr. Lake (to witness) : It was Mr. Norman you told it to was it not ?—Yes. The Chairman: Who wrote the paper 2—Mr.Osborne. Mr. Davies (to Mr. Lake) : You must withdraw your assertion. You aspersed Mr. Norman by saying he acted in two capacities. Mr. Lake: I know Mr. Norman too well to asperse him.

Eva Yates, and Annie Hunt scholars gave evidence corroborating the testimony of the previous twa wit- nesses. Laura Beckett, of 13 Hope-street, ss.id she went to chapel. In reply to the Chairman she said Miss Wood- ward was kind to her. She never, asked whaler she WM church or chapel. Miss Woodward had never asked the class to put their hands up for church or for chapee She was quite certain of this. By Mr. Davies: She was 9 years of age. She re- membered the day after the election, the poetry was " The poor fisher folk." Da you remember Miss Woodward saying something about toe electi eel—She asked 'who voted for the church. (Lattehter.)—Hew did they answer that ques- tion—by standing P—Tney put their hands up.—Did not she ask those to nut their hands up who went to chapel. Yes.—Did they ?—Yes.—Witness also put her hand up. The Chairman: What did you put your hand up for? —My Da voted for Church. (Laughter). Which did yoe vote for my dear ?—Far Church. But you go to Chapel generally, don't you ?—Yes sir. The witness repeated to the Chairman that the teaeher asked them ta put their hands up for Church and for Chapel. Lizzie Powaall, aged 9, said she was at school on the day after the election. She heard whe had WO3 from a boy at the Library before she came t school in the after- noon. In reply to the Chairman, she said Miss Wood- ward did not say anything about the electim in the class nor did she say anything about Church or Chapel. By Mr. Davies: Miss Woodward asked who went to chapel and said it did net matter whether they went to Churah or Chapel if they went to one. Miss Wo xl ward asked who went t) Chapel and the girls put their hands up. Miss Woodward did not ask the same question about the Church. Witness went to Church. The Church girls did not put up their hands. The Church girls did not laugh at the Chapel girls. She had not seen Mr. Davies nor his Clerk before. The Chairman : What day did you hold up yoar hands ?-e-Thursday afternoon. You told me nothing was said about church or chapel, didn't you P—No answer. Miss Woodward was now called, and said she was in 1 school on the day after the election teaching Standard IV as usual. In reply to the Chairman she said that she had heard coming to school that tee church had won. During the poetry lesson one child put her hand up and said the church had got in. Witness said "Yes and the Vicar is at the top." Then she added " We don't want election flow; we want our poetry." That was all that was mentioned about the elect:on. She did not ask the scholars to say whether they were c`nirei or chapel and tivy did not hold up their bands. She did not say that it was better they should go to chinch or chapel rather than be about the streets. The Chairmen : Hive you ever in course of your teaching or at any time, asked the children te hold up their ban is whether churith or chapel? I have aske them to hold up their hinds those who went to the Church Sunday Schoel.—When was that P—The Monday after the election.—What made you do that F—Because I was told by one of the teachers " You have got some naughty girls in your school." She said she wou,d see whether any of the girls in her class had been naughty. This was on the Sunday after the election. On the Mon- day she askA the girls who went to the Church Smday School, and told them that she had heard they had been naughty, and that she wanted to find out whether any of the girls in her class had been naughty. One girl blushed and she told her" You look as if you are

guilty" and the girl then said she was not naughty at all. She did not know whether the girl went to church or chapel—The Chairman: Did you ask them to hold up their hands ? —No.— Did you ask those who went to Church Sunday School ? —One girl put up her hand and said she went to chapel and I said It doesn't matter whether you go to church Or chapel so long as you go to church or chapel and not play upon the streets as I have seen some girls do."— Six children have all been saying you said that ?—I said 'that on the Monday.—You say distinctly and positively you did not tell them to hold up their hands at all on Thursday P—No.—Asked if she had any explanation to , offer. Miss W.;odward said she thought the children [ had mixed up what was said on Monday about Sunday school with the election. She had signed a paper without hesitation saying the had not done what was attributed to her. She maintained before the managers and those present that the allegation was incorrect. The nature of an oath was explained to witness and ,he said she was willing to take an oath bnause she was convinced she had not raid it. By Mr. Davies : She was willing to take the oath after what the six children had said.—ln reply to re- neated questions witness declared that she had not asked or a show of hands. She did not know there were any chapel children in the school until the Monday after the elec'ion.—You did not assume that they were all church children in that large building ?—I did until Monday.—You say that seriously ?—Yes.—No Non-con- formists at all P—No, I cid not know except Lillie Faulkner. I knew she was.—You took an interest in the election P—No, I did not. The Chairman now asked Min Towns, the Sunday school teacher, who had told Miss Woodward about the naughty girls and she confirmed Miss Wood ward's stet?... ment. • In reply to the Chairman Miss Sewell said there were between 30 and 40 children ready to be examined. The Chairman suggested calling these in a body, but Mr. Davies contended that they Fhould be sent for singly. The Chairman said they would call a few more and then they would know how far they need go. Annie Williams was called and examined by the Chair. , man said she remembered having to hold up hands to tell Miss Woodward who went to Sunday school and Miss Woodward said it was all right so long as they went to Sanday school. She did not know when she said this. Miss Woodward told them about children being naughty at Sunday school. She did not make them hold up their hands.lt was either the Monday or Thursday Miss Wood- ward talked about Sunday school. No one said " hands

p for church or hands up for chapel." A number of ther questions were asked the witness and the Chairman emarked that he thought her memory was not a very good one. Cross-examined by Mr. Davies: She remembered the poetry lesson " Poor flisherfolk " and she thought that was the day when the question was asked about the Church Sunday Schaol. Miss Woodward asked who had got in and they al shouted the Church had got in. She did not remember tands being held up, nor anything being said about Chapel. Miss Woodward had not seen her about this matter. The Chairman re-examined the girl, who made several contradictory statements. Mr. Davies remarked that this cut both of them. The Chairman: I think we need keep you no longer. Mr. Davies : No.

Alice Howard, 13, Victaria-road, said there was noth- ing said about holding up hands during the poetry lesson on the Thursday after the election,nor did they hold up hands on Monday. She had never been asked to hold up her hands for Church or Chapel. Her evidence was not shaken by cross-examination. _ _

Mabel Hewitt, was sent for as ths biggest girl in the class, and in reply to the Chairman said Miss Woodward talked to the class about Sunday school on both Thurs- day and M2niay. Miss Woodward did not ask anybody to bold up their hands either for church nor chapel. When Miss Woodward told them the churth had won she did not ask them to hold up their hands. Alter further questions the girl burst into tears and becoming calmer was cross-examined by Mr. Davies to whom she said Eva Yates, Maud Deakin, and Lillie Faulkner held up their hands. Lillie Faulkner said sOe went to chapel. This was in answer to a question from Miss Woodward. She did cot remember what the question was. Mr. Lake: Had it anytaing to do with children be- having badly in Sunday School ?—No sir, that was OR Monday.—Was it on Monday they held their hands up? —No, en Tuesday.—Oa Tuesday ?—No on Thursday.— Don't you know what it was about ?—No sir. Mr. Davies: What happened on Monday was separate from this ? Yes.

Miss Woodward recalled was impressively questioned by Mr. Davies, but maintained the truth oh her state.. meats, and repeated that the children had confused the Thursday with the Monday. She said on the Monday she made the inquiries because she wined to kuow who had been naughty at Sunday Scbool. Mr. Davies: Is it usual in a school maintained oy public money to inquire during the time allotted to eau. cation about what happened at Sunday school? Na answer.

Is it part of your duty —lt was my duty to see wha had been naughty. Certainly, if any ot my girls had been naughty. The Ctiairman : It is no use going from the general question. It is neither your business nor ours. Mr. Davies: I am going to deal thoroughly with the question. Mr. Lake said there was nothing at all in it. He sup. posed a teacher interested ia her children might ask them something about Sunday school. Mr. Davies: The children are singled out who had been naughty in church on the previous day. Ths Cnairinan : In all day schools it is the business to instil good manners. Mr. Davies: And to make the children stand up— The Cnairman : We should not in a °buret& school allow the church to be knocked down. The Chairman said there was no further evidence and be asked Miss Sewell whather she had confidence in the veracity of her teacher, and she said she had. He then ascertained from Miss Woodward the following informs. tion : She bad been at Runcorn 18 months, and came from Dalton in Furness National School. Before that eke was at Truro College. She was trained as a pupil teacher at Bunbury. She had numerous certificates as to her character. _ _

Mr. Davies now addressed the managers in which he reviewed the evidence of what he termed a most painful inquiry and claimed that the charge contained in Mr. Cooke's letter had been proved up to the hilt. lie con- tended that the managers could not now 864111Wis° the matter as absolutely false and without the slightest shadow of foundation. The Chairman : That is from our solicitor.—By the instructions of the managers. fie contended that be had proved the charge IR Mr. Coke' letter up to the hilt. The Chairman pointed out that the charge made in the railway carriage and to which Mr. Lake's letter re- ferred had not been proved. . _ _
Mr. Davies said ttiey were dealing at that inquiry with the charge formulated in Mr. Cooke's letter. He asked the managers not to shield themselves under the former statement.

The CSairman : We don't shield ourselves and I hope you will drop that way of expressing yourself. Are you bringing a charge against the managers P Mr. Davies said be would withdraw the words if un- parliamentary, but he pointed out that the charge was not against Miss Sewell but against Miss Woodward. The Chairman pointad out that Miss Sewell was the mistress over 300 children while Miss Woodward was one of a large staff. They bad dropped considerably from their original statament. Mr. Davies: I have not dropped from my original stateme at. The Chairman : Your client has. lidr.Laire said there was no foundation for the original statement._ _ _

Mr. Davies said the affair took place in Miss Sewell's school but they were dealing that evening with Miss Woodward, and he dwelt upon the seriousness of her offence, and Me. Norman and those who had acted with him bad done a public service in causing the matter to be investigated. Mr. Lake now delivered an address which he prefaced by saying he had not come there to make a speech, and now that the charge had been gone into it showed that it amounted to absolutely nothing. Nobody was an- noyed at it, and nobody would have thought anything about it if some individuals had not taken offence on their own amunt, and looked the matter up and magni- fied it. Be painted cut that certain children had given their evidence fairly and fluently, but as hero they came to children who had not been prepared, they found an amount of hesitancy, and an absolute lapse of memory which was far more nearly to his miad to t e what call- dren should be. Children could not remember from day to day what happened last week and Miss Woodward's explanation that the children had go:. confused between Thursday and Monday was highly probable. It was admitted by several witnesses that Miss Woodward asked those children who attended Sunday school to hold their hands up. Surely seeing that manners made the man, he was glad to see that in church schools manners were looked upon as matters of importance.. If children misbehaved themselves in or _

out of school, or in Sunday school, surely it was proper for the teacher to reprimand them and t(-aeh them some- thing better. The gravaman of the charge was what had been done was hurtful. There had b Ttl no evidence whatever to prove that and he concluded by saying there was no blame to be attached to Miss Woodward. The Managers then retired aad were abs,nt about half an hour. On returning the Chairman gave the verdict He said: The Managers have given the matter their' best consideration, and have for many h3urs gone into the investigation of every detail. They wish to say that in their opinion nothing has been done which caused or can rightly cause, any annoyance or pain to any Nonconformist child. They wiSa in the sec3nd place to say that in thi.ir opinion, some- thing was said on Thursday as to the election bu confusion appears to exist between what occurred an Thurs4ay and on Monday, in the ininJa of the chil- dren, and the managers cannot therefore, declare the charge proved. In the third place they wish to say that the subject of the inquiry has seemed to them to be very small and insignificant for an inquiry of this kind but that they felt it their duty, to bold the inquiry, in order to show the spirit of minims in which this school has been conducted and they mean always shall be conducted. The inquiry then concluded having occupied four houre and a half. •

div.head: BEFORE the IYIAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the IYIAGISTRATES.
MARGARINE SOLD As BUTTER.

At Warrington for ough Police Court on Monday be- fore Alderman Harrison (in the chair) and other magis- trates, Thomas Broadhurst, provision dealer, 82, Orford- lane, was summoned for selling, to the prejudice of In- spector Norman, butter containing 70 per cent, of fat, and not et the nature, quality, and substance pail for by the purchaser ; also for having exposed for sale a quantity of margarine, without having attached thereto a label, signifying it as such.—lnspector Norman said the first summons aral taken out under the sixth section of the Food and Drugs Act. Witness saw in a corner of the shop what appeared o be about twelve or fourteen pounds of butter. lie asked defendant to weigh him a pound, and when he had done so he paid for it, and told defendant that he would divide it into three parts, and send one away for analysis. He then asked defend- ant if he had any marzarine in the shop. He replied that he had not and never kept it. Witness subsequently sent the sample to th 3 county analyst, and received a certificate to the effect that it contained 100 per cent. of margarine.lt was adulterated with 70 per cent.of foreign fat. There was not a particle of butter in it. On re- ceiving the certificate he went to the shop and told de- fendant he would report him for having exposed for sale margar'ne without a label. Defendant told him that he had informed the person who supplied him with the butter of the In3pector's previous visit, and he had told him that he would stand by him. Witness next obtained a sample of butter frem the wooleaale dealer, and paid Is. for it. He submitted it in due course to the analyst, who certified that it was pure.—Defendant was repre- sented by his wife, who said that the wholesale dealer was to blame.—De'e -aslant was fined 403. and costs for the first offence and 20s. and costs for the second, in all £3 18s. The alternative of payment was two months' imprisonment.

ORDER TO DELIVER UP IE APPRENTICE.—AppI;CatIOD was made by the Liverpool Red Oxide Company for an order on Colonel E. J IL Spratt to deliver up an apprentice named Bamber —Evidence was given that Bember bad ab- sconded on the 12th November and a summons had been served on the commanding officer—The application was granted. A CASE DlSMlSSED.—Elizebeth Aldred. 206 Winwick-road, was summoned for committing wilful (Lamaze to a window on the 12th December the property of Harriett Barrett 202, Winwick-road.—Mr. Longion appeared for the defendant and pleaded not guilty.—The complainant said about a quarter past ten she heard the window broken, and saw the defendant walking away.—There was no other witness and the bench dismissed the case.

BUZ% MitginlS, Hoyle-street, Sum- moned has husband Rehari Maginis. 12 Worsley-street. for using threats to her on the 6th Dem oTher,....Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Clomplainant said they had nt been living to- gether and on the day in question defendant said he would knolls her brains oat and would kill her if she came near him again —As the evidence was unsupported the case was dis- missed.

THROWING A KETTLE AT I POLICE SERGEANT.—Mary Lockett. 4 Berry's-yard. was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Berry's-yard, at 10.40 on Saturday night' and with having assaulted P.S. Lawis at the same time.— Defendant pleaded not guilty.—P.S Lewis said a young man complained of having been assaulted by prisoner, who was drunk and covered with mud. Three young women and a man carried her home, and witness followed to get her name and address. When he got to the house defendant nicked up a jug and threw it at him. He warded the jug off. and she then said she would scald him. She picked up a kettle of boiling water and threw it at him. He jumped out of the way, but some of the water tell on his coat. P.O 's Healey and Howard came on the scene, and defendant was taken to the Police Station on a handcart. She would not walk.— P.C.'s Healey and Howard gave corroborotive evidence, and defendant was fined ss. and costs in each case. AM OBSENE Sol-la.—Thomas McDonald, 33, Hopwood- street ; Percy Arnold. 35. Hopwoo 1-street; Thomas Edward Phillips, 5, Derby-street; John Holmes, 45 Hopwood-street; and John James Norbury, 78, Battersby-lane, were sum- moned for using obscene language in Orford-avenue, on Sun- day, Dscernber 11th.—Def mdants pleaded not guilty —P.C. Cooper (38) said he heard defendants singing an obscene song in the avenue on the 11th December. He caught one of the defendants and he gave him the others' names. Defendants were fined la the costs 3s Sd each. A SUSPECTED LITNATiC —Margaret Lowry, last from St. Helens, a suspected lunatic, was charged with being found wandering in Horsemarket-street. at 1.15 a.m. on Sunday.— P.C. Howard (29) said the saw Lowry acting strangely in Hersemarketeitreet. He went to her, and she made several statements to him. She said she would ao away with her- self, as she was tired ef life. He took her to the Police Statlon.—The Chief Constable said the woman stated that she was formerly a domestic servant at S-aforth but left the situation about twe`vs months ago, owing to illhealth. She had since been In an Imbecile home.—The magistrates sent her to the Workhouse for medical examination. PiTCII AND Toss—William Crank (14), 32, Aikln-street ; William Stokes (13), 31, Leicester-street ; Prank Muir ( 2), 52, Aikin-street ; Sydney Ashton (12), 19, MEM-street, were summoned for playing pitch and toss near Aikin-street on the 11th December. They pleaded not guilty.—P C. Carter proved the case.—The lads were cautioned and fined 23 each. THE LIGHTING HEGULATION.—Richard Green and John Green, farmers, Lovely-lane, were summoned for not carry- ing lights attached to their vehicles at twenty minutes past five on the evening of December Bth in St. James-street, , Latchford. Defendants were each fined In the costs 3s 6d.— John Jaekson, milk dealer, 32. Dial-street. was summoned for a similar offence at Market-gate on the same date and also fined in the costs 3s 6d. TUBSDAV.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman). Councillor Shaw Green, and Mr. T. Birchall. THREAT TO SHOOT A. WlFE.—Martin Dooley was charged with making use of threats tower is his wife on December lst.—Defendant's wife said they w ,re lodgings and he broke in the house and after destroying blankets and other things said he would shoot her if he had a revolver.—The bench bound him over for six mon ha and ordered him to pay the costs or In default go to gaol for seven days.
