div.head: ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A WARRINGTON TAILOR.
div.p: THE ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A WARRINGTON TAILOR.
PRISONER colnurrED TO VIE SESSIONS.

Att-t-tt-e-Warringtoa Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning, before Mr„ Garnett (chairman), Mr. Birch&ll, and Councillor Shaw Green, George Parr, formerly a salesman for Messrs. Boydell Bros., tailors, 21, Sankey- street, WRS charged on remand with making false entries in his books with intent t o defraud. Mr. Browne ap- peared to prosecute and Mr. Jenkins defended. Mr. Browne said very serious offences had been coma- mited whilst prisoner had been in the employ of Messrs. Boydell Bros., who o 'fined a large number of shops, and had to depend upon the honesty and truthfulness of each inaividual manager. Prisoner had been in their employ for about tea years, and they hid the utmost confidence in him until tiey suspected him lest Christmas time. They wer • only proceeding wi h a few charges, as it I was proposed to take the case to Liverpool Quarter Sessions instead of the Assizes. 'fne amount enaoezzled Was altogether £250. J. H. Boydell, of the firm of Messrs. Boydell Bros., said prisoner had been in their employ since June,lBB9. For a period of twelve menthe he represented them at St. Helens until they opened a business at Warriagtoa. Witness found nothing wrong until he heard prisoner hid given himself up to the police, about a year ago. He was then of the opinion tint the amo ant taken was only paltry, and lee did not prosecute. fai saner was ill for abut a fortnight afterwards, and witness visited him at his house. and he then admitted having wronged the firm of £llB 17s. ed. In consequence of prisoner's wife's pleading he took prisoner on again as salesman at a salary of 30e. per week, and advanced his wages in March to £2. He believed prisoner was doing his duty until July, when he disc leered that be was again ape prepriating money. Witness then discharg id prisoner, and subsequently put the books into an accountant's hands. It was prisoner's duty to keep the order or day book journal, anti on their invoices were the words : "a printed receipt will be given ; no other recognised." The receipt produced, which Was not a printed one, was given by prisoner to Mr. W. H. Parkinson for an ac- count amounting to £2 155,, and Mesers.tloydell had not received the money. He had only found out the era- banement within the m eith. In the ledger produceden prisoner's handwriting, was a debit of £3 7s. 61. to Mr. liebert Turner, and another item for 121, 81., making altogether £l. It was prisoner's I duty to transfer the amount t) another folio, but he had I not done so. Witaese discovered within the last month that Mr. Turner had paid his account. 'fhere was also a receipt in prisoner's handwriting for £l, dated July 15-h, 1896, which ought to have been a printed receipt. The money had not neen accounted for, and ought to have been entered in the counterfoil book. Under date I January 17th, 1895, there was no enter of £215; 31 from Mr. Edwin Bradshaw. He predeced the receipt in prisoner's handwriting for that amouet, which al,o ought to have been a prirated one. It was prisoner's duty if he had received any money to entry it in tee daily takings book, and that amount had not been ac- counted for. He only discovered that amount on the accountant going through the books. The three items were only samples ot similar cases. Prisoner's earnings in 1895 were £2 les 111 (on an average) per week after paying all expenses, and the Paine in the following year In 1897, he drew £2 10s per week.—By the Chairman : During prisoner's defalcations did he volunteer ane information with re- ference to the money P In January, when ill,prisoner confessed to takine £llB, and he furnished the names of people from whom he had taken inoney.—By Mr. Jenkins: In January he first found out on prisoner's statement that something had gone wreng,. The system of audit had broken down, and he afterwards made a fresh system of checking. He m ght have asked pri- soner's wife where he went to se s prisoner if she had £2OO by tier, Sh 3 offered him £lO, which was in the Co-operative Seciety. He did not make any arrange- ment with Mrs. Parr as to tee payment to her husband of 5 per cent, on the turnover. Prisoner was told by the firm In January that if he stopped out of Warrington be would not be prosecuted. If the check system hid been carried out properly, the defrauding would have been fo end out carder. Mr. David West, chartered ace ountant, Manchester, said he was instructed in September last by 111°S3IS. Boydell Bros, to go taroagh ths books which had been kept by the prisoner, who hid three different systems of wrongly keeping them. One system was of entering in the day book journal as having posted unpaid accounts to a folio in the ledeer, whereas there was no entry in the ledger at sueh a folio. Prisoner had wronge I the firm of £6O under that system. The second system was to transfer items from one folio to another in the ledger, and £34 3; hid been taken in that way. The third system was to omit to enter accoun's in the daily takings book, and in that way £39 is had been taken.— By Mr. Browne : There was no blame attaehed to the firm for the way in which the books hid been kept.—By Mr. Jenkins : If the beues ea.! oeen audited oftener the the money abstracted would have been discovered sooner.
Prison.r said, in an3wer to the charge, "I reserve my defence."

FARMER.

INQUEST AND VERDICT. On Tuesday afternoon, at the Police Parade Room', Warrington, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of Peter NA•cott, (43), farmer, of Finger Post Farm, Manchester-road, Warrington, who met his death hy falling from a hay-loft, on Monday evening.— Et zabeth Morcott, v;dclow, was the first witness called. She last saw him alive abut Ginner time the same day. They were unloading hay from a cart in the loft when a boy came in and asked her to come and help to carry her master in, Shs weat and found her husband lying underneath the bin in the hay bit. He lay on his back with his face towards a ladder leading up to the loft. Re had never had an apopl4ctic seizure before, but had had rushes cf blood to the head. He was a very stout man. tile was not insured at all.—Detective Barlow said Dr. AL:Cathy had t)ld him that be (the Motor) had seen the dceased often, that he had rushes of blood to the head, and he would have thought ha was subject to apoplexy. Witness had examined tie bA7 but there were no marks on it.—Thomas Ellison, a farm labourer, was also examinsd,but as he was vary deaf and of weak intellect, nothing was elicitld further than that he w mt cllwn the ladder firs%and his master followed and lea.— Edward Whin's', a farm hand, said his master gave him a pike( from the loft into the cart, and asked Ellison if he could manage to get down. Five minutes after Ehi- son sholtel to him, and he went ti the bin where the deceased lay. Ho thought his [natter rnuit have slipped when coming down the ladder backwards. There was a good thickries of hay underneath which he fell UDO 1.— The jury returned a verdict of" Death from Natura Causes."
WARRINGTON FIELD CLUB.

At the sixth meeting ot the winter se•sion Dr. Billups read a paper entitled " Development se,i structure of a moss plant." A large and beautifully mounted series of =KAM enabled members to understand something of the form, colour, and variety of these plants, whilst their anatomy and life history were elucidated by diagrams, sketches, micrwcopic specimens, and museum models, With admirable lucidity Dr. Billups brought before his audience the stages in the life cycle of typical moss plants, adverting in pissing to the evidences of relationship which"tho 48 stages present, on the one hand to the signs and fungi, on the other to ferns, horsetails, and more remotely to the highest flower- ing plants. He emphasized the alteration of genera- tions RO evident in mosses and ferns, in the former of which the sexual whilst in the latter the asexual is the predominant generation, and asserted that wherever sex appeared atnengst plants this altera- tion could be detected. Br. Billups was warmly congratulated during the discussion which followed his paper, and a general wish was expressed that he would follow the subject up on a future occasion.

Warrington managed t secure another couple of points on Saturday, their victim; being Stockport, but it was only by a narroß margin that the homesters won. The Cheshire men have had a very rough time of it so far is toe Lancashire Leagu and were expected to fall a somewhat easy pray to the '6 wirepuders," bat as events turned out it took ties latter all their time to stave off defeat. Stockp3rt were not strongly represented, being witnout the services of Hoggarth (full back), Woraley (threequarter), and Booth (half back). Warrington turned out a 3 chosen with the exception that Allen took the place of &shunt who is undergoing a fortnight's suspension. The weather was worse for the spectators than the players, for a steady drizzle made thiogs rather unpleasant to those sten ling still. Tnough there hal been a lot of rain the turf was in excellent order and afforded a good footing. Mr. Ashton (Werneth) was the referee, the tetras being cemp need as follows: Warrington : Hallam, full pack ; Fish, Holcroft, Isherwood and Harris, threcguarters; Bate and Allen half backs; Naylor, B)ardmets, Fairhurat, Eden, Jolley, Swift, Scholtze, and Sudlow. forwards. . . .

_ Stockpert Granger, full back ; San is, Saville, and Veraon,threequarters;Bellamy and Robinson,intis:er, half backs; Gersile, Hallworth, Burrows, Wrigley, Collins, Davi isen, Brirnbl t, and Hague, forwards. There was very little wind, so that the choize of ends which fell to the Warrington captain, was of slight im- portance. Saville started the game, and after a couple of ex- changes Isherwood punted to Varnoa who mulled the wet ball, and Fiala racine up secured and scored a sen- sational try behind the poets a minute from the start. Holcroft was entrusted with the place kick, and landed a goal. Again Saville started from centre and this time it was Isherwaod's turn to fail in catching the ball, and Bate had difficulty in saving on the has. Penalties agaiast both sides left play at centre where Bate passel out to Isherwood, the latter making a grand run only to have it spoiled through the greasiness of the ball which slipped from his hands as he passed to Holcrofe. Sirnister dodged round the scrimmage and after a good run handed to Saville who got within a yard or so of the home line before being overhauled. The game quickly travelled back to the Stockport end where Eden had a good chance of scoring after a forward rush but knockea on. Vernon again let his side down but Robinson came to the rescue with a neat punt. Stockport were not daunted by their reverse and forced Warrington back. Hallam was taekled in possession and the homesters had to defend. Sitnister tried hard to get through but was well watehed by Bate. Allen at last punted out, Granger making a mark which Saville failed to improve upon. Playing in the Warrington half, Simister got away nicely, and neat transfers by Saud 9 and Robinson resulted in the latter racing in near ttie corner. Saville again failed at goal. Hardly had the game resumed be- fore Fish mulled a fair catch, and having no time to recover, the bill came into Wrigley's possession and was soon planted over the line. lads rapid change in the fortunes of the game was by no means to the liking of Warrington,. who were now a point to the bad. Though Warrington attacked again before the iaterval they were easily repulsed and Stockport maintained their lead up to half time.

The second half was a desperate struggle for supre- rnacy. Saville early gave Stockwrt an advantageous position with a hug,o punt. Robinson broks away with a dribble an' had a glorious chance spoiled threugh the ball rolling in tonne. The home forwards returned to the attack with vigorous play, and Robinson and Sands were both Ity.:kg in savior; from desperate rushes. While pressing severely Warrington were a vvareed a penalty kick u3ar the posts, but Isherwood could not pilot the ball ov-r the b kr. Give and take play followed. Fish shineing promineutly with good work for Warring- ton. He twice made plucky attempts to get through, and by his exertions Warrington were able to keep up the attack. Another e lay chance was given teem of obaining the Iced, but Ho!croft was no more successful with the kick than leherwood. After being mnnentarlly repulsed Warring- ton came back again, a splendid dribble headed by Nay- lot and Beariroan carrying play 0 the Stockport line , Granger saving in the nick of tene. The spectators had almost given up all hopes when Bats secured from a scrimmage, and dodging b sautifully he obteiaed the winning try amid vociferous cheering. No goal resulted. Stockport now lost heart and were h srd pressed to the close, Harris and Fish both being nearly in, while Jolley had a grand chance spoiled by Robineon, who was too speedy for him. The final score was : Warrington, one goal, 2 tries (8 points) ; Stockport, 2 tries (8 points).

Mr. William Long, J.P., presided at the annual meet- ing of this bank, held at the Savings Bank Buildings, Warrington, on Tuesday morning. There wore also present :—Mr. John Geddes (vice-chairman) Revs. John Yong,e, W. IL Drarnmond. Richard Greenall, Messrs. C. Jackson Eiolmes, John darri,.on, William Tinsley, D. W. Finney, John Peers, John Dewhurst, George Dakin, and James Wood, with Mr. Thomas Tunstall (actuary). Mr. F. MONKS wrote to the chairman apologising for his inability to attend.

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The report of the bank read as follows :—"ln present- flog the general statenterat of accounts of the bank for the year ended 20th November, 1898, the Committee of Management have much pleasure in drawing attention to the very satisfactory progress of the business of the bank. During the year 928 ace sunts have been opened, making the total number of depositors 12,020. 23,001 transactions were recorded as compared with 21,113 last year ; showing an increase of 1,891. The increase in the amount owing to depositors in the same period is £8,297 94 83, making the total amount now due to them £335,309 3s id, in addition to which there are investments on their on behalf to the extent of £8,359 Os 6.1,-21 per cent consolidated stock. The assets of the bank are £340,436 103 103, showing a sur- plus of £5,127 7s 93, after deducting the whole sanount due to depositors. The National Deft Commissioners hold on behalf of the Institution a sum of £336,778 Is2d which is considerably in excess of the total liabilities. The extracttd list of depositors'balances,certified by the Auditor, is placed on the counter during the hours of busioess, and any depositor may satisfy himself, by its inspec ion, that the amount to his credit, in accordance with his pass-book, is certified to the Go ernment. The Bank is opetadaily for the transaction of business, and sums as low as one shilling are received. Fifty pounds may be deposited in any one veer until the amount to the credit of the depositor r 'aches £2OO. A furtner £2OO may also be received in any ve a for iavestmtnt in Government Stock. Payments not exceeding £lO are made on demand, larger amounts are paid subject to a week's notice. The continued steady increase in the number of depositors' accounts, and in the numb°, of transActlons, is a most , grstifying feature of the work of the bank. The greater proportion of the transactions are of small amounts, which goes to show that the bank is taken advantage of by the class of depositors for a hose benefit the Ituititu- Urns was established in the year 1818. There are 4,794 depositors whose accounts do not erceeed £l. For the Committee of Management, Wrza.rs.or LONG, chairman ; JOHN GEDDES, vice-chairman." The CIIAIRMaN said he need not detain them by many remarks, cer:ainly he need say nothing in advocacy of a bank which was made much use of by the poor of the town, and existed for the encourageme ,t of ihrdc. He noticed that it had been said at a meeting of one of their larger institutions in Manchester that " blessed was the instltation which had nothing to bring forward. It was dull and monotonous in ite report, but it indicated pros- oerity." That was cez taints, the case with them. They had a very good report before them. As they saw, there had been a steady increase in the number of dep.esicors' accounts, and the number of transactions, a very gratifsing feature of the work of the bank. They would all agree that the bank was more particularly intended for the workers of the town, and although their growth might not be as large as some might desire, still it was a fact that the greater propsrtion of the transactions were small amounts, which went to show that the bank was taken advantage of by the class of depositors for 1 whose benefit the institution was established in 1818. There were 4,794 depositors whose accounts did not exceed £l. That, of course, was very gratifying, and though they would like them to increase their accounts, it showed that the bank was used to a large extent by the poorest of the people. The transactions for the year, they would see, were about 2,000, or ten per cent, more than the previous year. Nine hundred and twenty- ' eight accounts had been evened, and the total number of their depositors was 12,020. The Actuary had pre- pared a roport showing that the working expenses were 4s. lop. for every £lOO, which was very satisfactory indeed. The report generally compared favourably with those of other banks of similar size.

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. RUIN YONGE said he had been asked to move a resolution touching the chairmanship and vice-chair- manship of the bank. There were instit,utions in which it was desirable that changes should be made with re- gard to the position of chairman. He thought,however, they would all agres with him that a savings bank was not one of those institutions. It was very important and desirable that the presiding officers, if he might so call them, of a bank like that should be the same gentle- men from year to year, ao long as they did noir work well. They Lad in Mr. Long and Mr. Geddes two gen- tlemen who had done admirable service since the time of their appointment, and he was sure they would de- sire, and all c -inflected with the bank would share that desire, that they should be prevailed upon to cottinue in office for another year. He, therefore, propossd their re-election. _

The Ray. H GancsaLL, in seconaing, endorsed Mr. Yonge's remarks. He felt slum tney were the right men in the right place. The motion wa.i unanimously carried _Mr. LONG, responding on behalf of himself and Mr Geddes, said they let deeply the honour the manager 3 did them in asking them to COntinue ia office. Daring the early days of his connection wits the hack he was of opinion that those positions sho'ild not b 3 held in continuity, and thst a change shmld take place OCC3 sionally, as new blood might bring more energy into th work. div.head: COUNCILLOR F. R. ROBE FITS AND SOCIALISNI.
div.p: COUNCILLOR F. R. ROBE FITS AND SOCIALISNI.

Sir,—What is the matter with Councillor Roberts? I notice from your issue of December 10th, that he is reported to have said, at the Shop Asshtants' meeting, the following words :—" Sir William Harcourt said some short time ago we are all Socialists now.' He (Mr. Roberts) would rot go so far ai to say everything Shouli follow out Socialistic ideas, but Sociaii,m had many germs of truth in it. Now, sir, at Mr. Waldron's lecture last Sunday afternoon, Mr. Rob 3rls in his capa- city as chairman uttered these remarkable words. "He did not believe in Socialism, for it was nothing else but simply absolute coercion." Now, how does he reconcile these statements. Ai a proclaimed " progresaive," we expect progress from him, but, sir, this s mnds like re- trosression,or, perhaps, Councillor Roberts has suddenly developed int a" new humorist." Horrid thought. for if so we shall certainly have to provide someone to tare care of him. On the bills advertising Mr. Waldron' lecture it was plainly stated that questions were invited, yet notwith- standing that siveral of the audience were prepared to ask q lestions on such an imp irtant subject, after three only had b,en put Mr. Rlbers sudienly put the closure on us by asking a gentleman on the platform to pro- nounce the banedictio3. I+ this conduct worthy of a Town Councillor?
FAIRPLAY.

div.head: TH.E REV. W 11. STABLE 3 ANS vVERS SIR JON
div.p: TH.E REV. W 11. STABLE 3 ANS vVERS SIR JON
BRUNN ER.

_ Sir,—! had no idea that I was such a formidable oppo- nent that no Runcorn Progressive dare tackle me, but that perforce the great Sir John himsalt mast be brought out. The little episode of " Sir John to the re3cue "reminds me of little boys who, when testy are fairly beaten in a fight, run home to their mother, and in whining tones cry" mother he has hit me." Than out c miles the. en- raged mother, and in loud and angry words, vows vengeance. Sir John is sometimes unfortunate in being badly informed. I am reminded of a certain queition he once asked in the Rome of Commons at the instance of certain buy-bodiee in which he enquired whether the Weston Parish Council might not have power given to it to appoint a trintee to the " Orred Charity." Wnat however mint have been his chagrin and how he must have blessed his informers when the governm-nt politely told him that all this had been done more than a year before, and that tee trust was being properly worked. Sir John suffers aeaire to-day from incorrect information. But to the letter—it is vary kind of Sir John to print my title and calling in full, so as to dis- tinguish me from my nennesake and re'ative in Leeds, but I area sure my kinsman will not thank him for it. As to Mr. Joseph Pritchard—if all the mean tricks his beats all—to try and make capital out of his sickness and to pretend to be his friend after the unkind way the Pregressives spo're of him earlier in the Eiectien. We have not forgotten that though Mr. Pritchard'e letter announcing his rA'rement in censeq lance of sickne3s was posted on the walls and distributed broadcast through the town, yet he was held up to ridicule as the " dropped" candidate. Sir John says I ma le Mr. Joseph Pritchard appear to be responsib'e for the haod- bill. He is probably ignorant of the fact that Mr. Joseph Pritchard hid already issued a letter signel by himself calling upon his supporter 3 to vote for Mr. Cunnioehern and announcing his retirement. But Sir John has been led into another mistake. He says" To print Mr. Joseph Pritchard s as to come as near as possible to Mr. James Pritchard" was a " petty trick" (1) as a matter of fact we printed it Jos Pritchard lone before Mr. Pritchard's retirement was even thought ()fond we had always done so for the con- venience of the printer. (2) But curiously enough I have looked up the original manuscript of the hand bill gent to the printer, and find that "Joseph" was actually written in full and that the printer altered it to "Jos " wholly for convenience in setting up the typo. Let no one misursderstand me. lam not seeking te thrust any blame upon the printer, far I hol I that th,re is no blame attaching to anyone in the matter. I only mention this to show how much Sir John has allowed liiinselt to be misled. Lastly Sir John says :—"Mr. Stables ha l defended his honesty at the expense of his inteligence." Well, it is something to know that I rim honest, and as tc my in- telligence, I leave the judgment of it to those who know me.—Yours &c.
W. H. STABLES.
Rancorn.
SOME THOUGHTS FOR THE SEASON.

- - Sir,—With what wiadom and goodneis ha 3 the Creator ordered the various phenomena of the circling year and attuned the minds of his intelligent creatures to per- ceive and enjoy the charms that are peculiar to each. The breezy Spring„with its lengthening days and bright- ening skies ; Summer,with its glorious sunrises and sun- sets, and Autumn, full of quiet loveliness, are all rich in objects that delight the eye and elevate the tboushts of all who take pleasure in the worSB of God. Nor are the phases of Winter less prolific in themes for gratefei admiration and joy, and my object in this letter is to depct some of the more striking of these phases. Winter differs from all the other seasons in that it is, for the most part, a time et gloom and desolation. Then the fields and meadows lie bars and spongy through long continued rains, and withered leaves and naked boughs are all that linger on to remind us of the verdure and bloom of the previous months. But then Winter has aspects of her own which lend a charm and a glory to her darkest and most mmotonous days. How often will streams of golden sunshine break through the creviced clonal, revealing the calm blue skies beyond, and gladdening tne dreary. landscape and the shivering birds with hopes of retnrnins spring. Then how grand, how sublime is the spectacle presented by heaven and earth when the Storm King rides upsn the rolling cloud,! Then the works Of men quail bebre Him, the forest bends and moans under His invisible lash, and the seas, tossed into huge billows, crash upon the shore with the noise of thunder ! But Winter often shakes his hoary locks over the deso- lated hills and valleys, and covers them with virgin snow. And never does the world look so beautiful as when it is thus arrayed. So exquisitely formed and so , stainless in this robe, and so completely dos it conceal all blemishes that the feet of Angels might tread upon it as they do upon the pure fields of Heaven. In the early mornings, while the stars still twinkle in the sky, what a joy it is to walk abroad upon this white word then hardened and consolidatA by the breath of frost, and watch the sun slowly rise above the horizon with the first streaks of returning day. So profound is the silence then, and so weird like and mysterious the ap- pearance of the whole scene around us that, with a little stretch of imagination, we might fancy that a new and sinless world had dawned upon us. The crowning glory of winter, however, is its starry skies. When day is ended, and the clouds have been rolled back by some secret power, then the vast concave of heaven stands out revealing a universe of stars of all magnitudes and of all degrees of glory. With what deep awe and wonder do we look up to those mysterima orbs, longing to penetrate the secrets of their origin and des- tiny, and feeling the while an overpowering sense of the insignificance of man in the scale of creation. Alas] yet those stars were made for man, and have shined upon his path, ani watched over his habitation for six thou- sand years at least. Go where he will, at home or abroad, on land or on sea, he feels their presence cheer- ing him in the gloom and solitude of night, and raising his adoration to that unchanged and unchangeable Being whose creatures they are as well as himself. And when his life passes from the seen to the unseen, from the present to the etarnel state they will look down upon his grave to long as. a vestige of it remains in existence. And, lastly.winter brings U 3 the holy season of Christ- mas when devout minds love to commemorate the first advent of the Redeemer of the world. And how closely associated were the stars of heaven with that wonderful event. The eyes and thoughts of the shepherds of Bethlehem were,doubtleis fixed upon the glorious firma- ment when they heard the wonelerous announcement that Christ, " the bright and morning star," had risen upon the earth. Ant was it nol; a star that led the wise men Irons their homes beyond the Euphrates to worship that Christ in a lowly Khan at Betilehem ? fire angelic song of peace and good will to men which accompanied tile ravelation of tee Savicur's birth never seem% 99 sweet and so full of meaning as is does when we look up to the starry skies of Christmas. While thus engaged do we not seem to hear it floating over the everlasting bin ? while in many an ivied lane and lowly cottage glad voices join in the glorious strain. Yours truly, lONA.

In connection with the agitation in progress throughout the country on the question of disarma- ment as set forth in toe Czar's rascript, the follow- ing resolution was passed on Sunday by the scholars of the Congregational Sunday School, Newton:— That the scholars of the Congregational Sunday School, Newton-le- Willows, earnestly call upon Her Majesty's Ministers to energetically support the Peace Conference in securing a truce of God among the nations, an arrest of the increase of armaments, ant an international agreement that hencefortn Governments will always invite mediation before appealing to the sword. (Signed on behalf of the Sunday School), Henry Law, superintendent ; Moses Battersby, Douglas McHardy, secretaries.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A—WARRINGTON CARTRR. Mr. F. Turner (deputy coroner) held an inquest at the Cheater General Infirmary on Monday on the body of Robert Buckley, 37 years of age, a carter, residing at Battersby-lane, Warrington.—gr. Draper, of the firm of Robert Davies and Co., solid.. tors, Warrington, appeared on behalf of Mr. Ralph Johnson, the employer of deceased.—From the evidence given it appeared that deceased was employed on Wednesday to cart a load of furniture from Warrington to Hatton Heath, near Chester. He had a spring cart for the purpose, and started on his journey ab nooa. At G2O .he same even- ing he met George Elall, a fellow employe, at the Chester Station,and together they continued on the journey. Both of them rode on the cart, and when near Christleton Bridge, the deceased, who was driving, in attempting to get off the cart fell under the wheel, which passed over his chest. His com- panion immediately ran to his help and deceased, with assistance, walked to the Trooper Inn, which was close by. Here he complained of feeling very much hurt, but refused to see a doctor. Ultimately. however, Dr. Wright was called in, and deceased was at once sent to the Chester Infirmary in the doctor's vehicle. On his admittance there, about ten o'clock, it was found that he was suffering from fractured ribs and fractured breast bane, his right lung also being damaged. Els died on Friday night, about 9.30, from pneumonia, in consequence of his injuries. The jury returned a verdict of" Acci- dental death."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, DECEMBER 23 1r)98,
FUNERAL OF LORD NEWTON. QUIET WMEHONY AT DISLEY.

The funeral of the late Lard Newton took place at Disley on Tuesday afternoon, and in accordance with the expressed wish of the deceased nobleman, the cere- mony was of a very quiet and simple character. It was attended, h wever, with every manifestation of the r,- speet and esteem ia which his lord.hip was held, not only by residents ire the immediate district,but by many others with whom he had been associated in life. Since Saturday the body has lain in the private chapel a: Lyme Hall,enclosed in a polished oak coffin with plain brasi furniture. The 'late was inicribed : William John, First Baran Ne wton, Born D member 19th, 1828, Died December 15th, 1898.

Sh ortly before the hour fixed for toe interment the coffin was p aced in th 3 hearse and a cortege was formed up in froat of the Hall. Ininediat sly after the hearse canna the coaches conveying the chief mourners, Lord Newton (the successor to the title), arid Lady Newton, the Hon Sloyl Legh. Major and Mrs. Gilbert Leg,h, Major and Mrs. W. Rowley, Mr. Piers F. Legh. Copt tin Legh, the Rev. Canon Whittiegten, Mr. El. Houseman (the family solicitor), and Mr. J. E. Pardy (the estate agent.) Tne mourners were immediately followed by the servants of the houeetrold and the estate, and in this order the procession moved off t iwards the church. At the park gates the tenantry of the estate were drawn up on either side to allow the cortege to pass through, and then tined in at the rear and accompanied it to the church. On arrival there the coffin was borne up the nave by six workmen employed on the estate, and they were suoported on the right by Mr. W. Trevor (house steward), and on the left by Mr. Eirseman (his lordship's valet), with Mr. Garsewell (farm bailiff), and Mr. Gibs in (gardener), behind. rhe first portion of the burial service was cendueted ins the church, the officiating clergy being the Rev. C. J. Sattsrthwaite (vicar of Dialey), the Rev. W. Symonds (rector of Stockport), the Rev. C. Goodall (High Lane) the Rev. T. G. Cox (curate of Disley), and the Rev. G. N. Wilmer kvicar of Norbury). Tee choir was in atten- dance and led the singing of the hymns " Now tee Labourer's Task is o'er," and " For all rhy Saints," ap- p Anted by the vicar to be sung at the special request of the family. Mr. H. Nicholson presided at the organ and played as the congregation was as-iernbling and leaving the church. The interment afterwards took place in the family fault on the south side of the churchyard, in which already lie the late Lord Newton's undo and two brothers. Several private c irrlages joined in the procession as it left the park, and amongst others were those of Kr M Woodiness (Comastall), Miss Hudson (Aarple), Mr C S Hoar (Dislev), and Mr James Murray (Dislev). Wreath; crosses, and other floral tributes were sent by the Dowa- ger Lady Newton, Lord and Lady Newton, the Honour- ably Sibyl Legh, Mrs Rowley, Mrs Gilbert Legh, Major Gilbert Legh, and Major Rowley ; Mr and Mrs Piers Legh, Captain and the Mi•ises Legh, the servants at Lyme Hal, the gardeners at Lyme Hall, the farm em- ployes at Lyme, the Norbury tenants, the Lyme, Han I- ley,and Disley tenant farmers, toe Newt on Conservative Association, Mr J E Pardy and Miss Pardy, Mr House- man, Mrs Milligan, the Duchess of Buckingham and Ciandos and Eirl Egerton, Frau Von Stamford, Colonel and Mrs W Lowther. Mr and Mrs Leigh Slater, Mrs Hudson, the Rev C J and Mrs Satterthwaite,Mr and Mrs J Platt (Cheadle), Sir Francis Astley Corbett, Mr and Mrs Lawrence Currie, the Earl and Countess of Elles- mere, Eizaheth, Countess of Wilton, the Disley Goli Club, the lisley Cricket Glob, and Mrs Preston. Seeing that it was Lord Newton's earnest de iire that he should be buried as quietly and with as little demon- stration as possible, no invitations were issued for the funeral, but it was understood that all who wished to attend were heartily welco.ne to do so. Among those present in the church were Lord Penrhyn, Mr. Gilbert Claughton, the Rey. R. E. Broughton (vicar of Prest- bury), Mr. T. Hardcastle Sykes (Cheadle), Colonel Fern- ley (Buxton). The Disley Rural District Council and the Disley Hor- ticultural Society were amongst the public bodies repre- sented, and there WAS a large gathering of the general public. The church lo>ll was tolled for an hour or so be- fore the time appointed for the ceminencemeat of the service, and b lids were drawn at most of the private houses ant places of business is the village. The following local gentlemen attended the funeral : Mr. T D Grimkii•Drayton, Mr W Holland Owen, Mr W A Mawisley(reor-se ating Newton Division Censervative Association), Mr C 3 P Borron and Mr W W Shirley (representing Newton Urban Comeil), Mr T J Gillespie, Mr R Stone, Dr C T S:reet, Mr G Clark,Mr F A Frost,Mr J W 'll lorp, Mr W Long,ton,Mr Abbott,Mr C Coventry, Mr .1 Crolichlev, Rev J Carson, Rev T R Matthews, Mr T H Suttoo (Warrington), Mr J R Lloyd, and Mr E Pilkington (St. Helens).

Some tricky play on the par; of Whitehouse enabled the viii- tore to get into the home half and Hayes had to concedc a corner. The viritors next hKI a turn at attacking and Whitehouse shot hard at Chew when he had a clear goal, the custodian bringing off a grand save. Just before the interval the homesters again took up the attack and Smith •h at into the n•t, but the whistle had previously gone for offside, and half time arrivsd with a blank sheet. Immediately on resuming the homesters weat down th 3 field with a rush and a*fine piece of work On ' the part of Leach and Settle resulted in the former al- most getting through.Earlt stown still cantinued to have the best of the argument and they p,nnerl the County in their own quarters, Leach eventually banging the ball into the net, giving Topping no chance whatever. The second goal followed soon afterwaris, this corning from the foot of Downes. The game now tone I down considerably, Earle•town having matters all their own way, and Hampson soon scored the third goal with a beautiful shot. Final E attest° cvn 3, Wigan COanty 0. Even the most expectant of the home supporters never anticipated smth an easy victory, and had the weather been fine, there is no doubt the score would have been heavier.

There were others higher oe the ladder of emineece in his profession, with higher gifts to rivet the attention of the people or to wield at will the passions and emotions of the people, but he knew of no one in eorinection with the stage wnose life had been so essen- tially blameless, and so faithful b wife and children and so loyal to Or promptings of duty than the deeeased gentleman. Human society would never shot itself off from the realization of any true art, or indeed ought it Ito do se. The stage ha] stood fir 3,00 years bee tU3e !it had a basis in human nature. Society would not drop it, but he trusted would demand that it shonld rise to its own s'andards and be as pure as itself. Decent people would have a decent stags. Percy Mit en en- deavoured to give to the people amusements that were Pure and innocent, clever and exhilare'- ine. From many quarters, as the wreaths would show' came the recognition cf his worth. Brotherly, affeceienate, and loyal, he had many friends among his brethren. His name was safe in the keepiog of the undying mem oriee of every heart that enjoyed the privilege af his friendship. He was 41 id to kuOW that when on the borderline of eternity he re,t upon the great love of God. When enduring excruciating agony with fortitude and patience he faced eternal r eali- ties with a triumphant faith in the infinite love. Let him (tho speaker) say to his comrades, doubt as they might, despair as they might, in the solemn moments of life, when sorrow came and sickness laid ite hand upon them and death loomed before them, the imp 'rishable instinct of their nature would assert itsef, the humen spirit sighed for Gad. Dear Percy Milton found it so, and whispered in his awful agoniee the sweet words o God is Love." Let them so live that whets they passed away, and friendly lean is laid them in their grave, friendly hearts would nor be far wrong in thinking of them that they were staunch in an allegiance to the princioles of righteousness and truth. Many uncharit- able aril unkind things had been said of the honourable profession of which their dear brother was such a con- spicuous member, but let him say, in conclusion, after sincere thought and meditation, that in the great issue which lay SO near to them all it wou'd make lit++ differ- ence whether they left this world C atholics, Anehcens. or Nonconformists, professors of this religion or of the histrionic art, but it would make an awful difference if they went int, eternity real or not. He hoped his FO:- rowing comrades would endeavour to emulate Percy ' Miton's example, and Sweep the stage and all connected with it of its impurities, and help to give the people a , pure steer, and maki it a mighty moral factor in the life of our nation.

div.head: DEATII OF AIR. W-ALLA.CE REVILL.
div.p: DEATII OF AIR. W-ALLA.CE REVILL.

Mo3t genuine regret will b 3 caused throughout the theatrical world, and particularly in S. El.deos nd Sheffold, by the death of Mr. William Wallis ("Wal- lace') Reyill, the popular proprietor of the Theatre Royal, Sc. Helens, liheflield, Leicester, and Derby, whica tniik place at Sh3ffitld early on Tuesday morning. Cpinicig so closely on the death of Mr. Reyili's eldest sou

who was buriedat St. Helens on Saturday, the sad event will be the more deplored. Mr. Revill comes of a well-keown theatrical family, his father being the prVtietor of the St ockport and Ashten-under- Lyno theatres, which are now carried on by Mr. Cnarles Revill, the eldest son. Mr. Revill's first venture was at Leicester, where he became lessee and the proprietor of the Theatre Royal. In 1884, Mr. Ravin leased the old St. Halals Theatre, sittistJ near the top of Bridge-street, from Sir David Gamble. Under his direction the theatre became a great success,and Mr. Ravin purchased the property. A movement in favour of the building of a mora suitable aud commodious theatre sprang up, and Mr. Revill courageously faced the situation, and in the year 1889 begrn to build the splendid new theatre in Corporation- street, which has since been pronounced by Mr. Wilson Barrett, Mr. J. L. Toole, and other eminent actors to be one of the be,t theatrical buildings out of London. The opening of the theatre in August, 1889, attracted the greatest attention, and it has proved a great sumees. Mr. Re.vill subsequently sold the old theatre to the Salvation Army, and le.'er told the Circus in North-road, which was his property for a conaderable time. During recent years Mr. Reyill extended the scope of his opera- tions, and took over the large theatre at Sheffield and later one at Derby. Along with Mrs. Revill, who took an active parr in her husband's work, Mr. Revill was most highly respected in all these parts, and his sod lea death in the mt Ist of a busy and prosperous carer will be most deeply regretted. Mr. Revill was only taken ill on the 10th ire. At the funeral of his son on Saturday it was stated that Mr. and Mrs. Revill were unable to attend,owing to shock,but the real reason was that Mr. Revill was suffering from a severe attack of the fatal malady which had carried off his son.

div.p: FASEIIONIBLE WEDDING.

MR. HAROLD 110300 E BRUNNER, AND MISS ETHEL HOUSTON. On Saturday afternoon, at Christ Church, Pad- dington, London, in presence of a very large and fashionable assembly, many of whom had come specially from the provinces far the ceremony, the marriage took place of Mr. Harold Roscoe Brunner, son of Sir John Tomlinson Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, of Druid's Cross, Wavertrae, Liverpool, and 9. Ennismere-gardens, South Kensington, ant Miss Ethel Houston, eldest daughter of Mr. Arthur Houston, L.L D., q.c , formerly of Fitz williara-square, Dublin, and Elsinore, Dalkey, near Dublin. The church was, as usual, decorated with choice flowers and plants. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. J. C. Ridgeway, M.A., Vicar, assisted by the Rey. E. Bauverie Day, M.A., Chaplain to her Majesty's Forces at Woolwich, and the service was fully choral. The bride was accompanied by her father, Dr. Houston, Q.O , who conducted her to the chancel rails, and in due course gave her away. Mr. Ernest Brunner, brother of the bridegroom, acted as best man." There were six bridesmaids attending the bride—Miss Olive Houston, Miss Vera Houston (sisters of the bride), Miss Maud Brunner and Miss Effie Brunner (sisters of the bridegroom), Miss Margaret Tomlinson, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. James Tomlinson, of Willington•hall, Che- enire ; and Miss Olive Told, daughter of Dr and Mrs. Todd, of Drumahoe, Lendonderry—wao were charmingly gowned, and they also wore unique hats of black velvet, with black ostrich. plumes in front, fastened with paste buckles and arranged with pale pink and scarlet carnations under the brim. The bridegroom's presents to them were gold pencil bangles studied with turquoises, sapphires, and diamonds, and instead ot the usual nosegays they carried muff s arranged with violets and carnations, completing an exceedingly hand- some bridesmaid's costume. The bride looked remarkably well in a wedding gown of white duchesse satin, embroidered in a design of true lover's knots in jewels, and covered with rare old lace, her full Court train of same satin else em- broidered with true lovers' knots, arranged from the shoulders. Her veil of exquisite lace covered a tiara of real orange flewers,and her ornaments were diamonds, the gift of Lady Bruuner,and she carried a nest bridal bouquet of rare ex sties, tie I with white satin streamers. The musical service was finely conducted, the hymn "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden," and the Psalm "God be merci- ful to us and bless us" and " 0 perfect love, all human then t transcending," anal " Lead us, Heavenly Father, lead us," being rendered with great effect. Afterwards Mr. and Mrs. Roscoe Brunner left for the Riviera for their honeymoon tour. The reception held at 22, Lancaster-gate was vary largely attended. div.head: ST. THOMA.S CHARM-, HALTON.
div.p: ST. THOMA.S CHARM-, HALTON.
THE VICAR AND HALTON PARISH COUNCIL

The annual distribation of the St Thomas' Charity took place at the Girl's School, Haltoa, on Wednesday, when there were present ;—Rev G D Wray, Messrs C L Evans. J Jeacock, J Looker, T Wright, J Hatton, J Ackerley, and A Woodier. The Vicar having been appoiated to the chair sail his attention had been drawn to a report of the proceedings of the Halton Parish Council at a meeting held on the Bth December, during which a letter was read by the clink concerning St. Thonals' Charity which he had written, as clerk to toe Coun;;il, io the editor of the " Councillor." Fle was surprised at reading that letter because of • the errors it contained,—srrors of t and misrepresentations, which it was difficult to account for. Further it cm- tamed an insinuation which was a fiction of a mind unhealthily imaginative. To begin with the letter declared that " Part of the will states that it" (that was St. Thomas' charity) " must be distributed in the pre- sence of the Vicar, wardens, and principal inhabitants," whereas the only memorandum of that point was to the effect it was " intended hy the donors to be distributed early on the feast of St. Thomas among the deserving poor of the township of Halton in such manner and pro- portion as should b 3 thought proper by the ministers, chapel v ardens, and priacipal inhabi'auts, the security ' being in possession of Sir Richard Brooke of Norton Priory." By that he understood that the charity was to be distributed by the Vicar and wardens and principal inhabitants and not merely in their presence as the statement in the lefter implied ; no matter who held the securities. He thought it was very unfortunate that this memorandum should have been misquoted. The letter than stated that "last year previous to St. Thomas Day we (the !, Parish Council) recommended a widow to be added to the list." Whereas it should have been and he thought the minutes of the Paris Council would bear him out' "the Parish Council passed a resolution that a certain widow should be added to the recipients." He con- sidered that it was a decidedly stronger action than a recommendation, and that he would be right in pointing out to the Council that although the income of the charity was now paid to their account they had no power to definitely decide, nefore St. Thomas' day and apart from the vicar and wardens and principal inhabitants who were to be the recipients of it. Be had expressed his conviction that a recommenda- tion from the Parish Council of any person whom they thought deserving of help, would always receive a re-

npectful consideration from the administr store, and thought, p-irsonaly, that the m Trobrr3 of the Parish C p.incil could share ia the distribution by aMending as " principal inhabitants." It was a point h had einphasieed. He looked upon the insinuation contain id its tho lector of the Parish Council in t e sontene >a " the former p3llo' rl3 we think look upon us as intrudsra" and "are we simply lookers- on as inferred ?" as mischevious ana totally uncalled for. flo had not uttered one single won I to justify either seotene% Nor did he believe that the letter ex- pressed he opinion of anythinz like all the membirs of the Council. Indeed, hi was sorry th .t there should be even one who should be so suspicious of his motives. He though: it by no means uncommon for the securities of the funds of a cOarity to be in the hands of one set of persons an i the adminiAration of the income in the hands of another set of persons and while the Lolal Gwerninent Act of 1891 provided, with the approval of the Charity Coarnis loners for an increase in the number of tru,tees of such securities it did not as far as he hsd read the Act alt ir the administration of such charity.. . _

Mr. Look-;r in reply sad he thouzlot the objec; of the Parish Council was to obtain further inforinaion as to their powers as regards the charit 7. He was quite sure that no one had any doubt about it having been distri- buted fairly in the past.. The Vicar thought it was quite right that the Parish Council should obtain all the information they could about the charity but took exception to the statements in the letter which implied that he was anxious to keep the Parish Council away from the distribution. Whereas the erect opposite was his wish. The letter gave a false impression to the public of the statement he had made. Mr. Evans explained that the Parish Council were now in exactly the Sims position as Sir Richard Brooke formerly held with respect to the charity, and drew at- tention to Section 14 (1) of the Lee ii G...vernment Act 1894 which states " where trustees hold any property for any public purpose connected wit l the parish thy can with the approval of the Charity Commissioners transfer the property to the Council. If the Council accept the transference they are to hold the property subject to the same trusts and conditions as the trustees held it." That had been done in the present case, and he thought the Parish Council could attend the distribu- tion as principal inhabitants as Mr. Wray had stated. He thought they had no no ne power in the distribution than any other inhabitant. . . .

Mr. Woodier said that he, as Clerk. hid written the letter becansa he thought it expres:-.e I thP feelings of what was said at the Parish Council me tin. It was intended to ask tor informatioe, arid hi did not think anything further was meant, Mr. Jeacock said th it when the Parish Council wis first formed they appointed a Committee who went blly into the charities and presented a report which was con- sidered satisfactory at the time. He was surprised that the matter hal again been brou.;ht up for discussion, as he thiniztit it was definitely sittled. The Committee then distributed £26 2s. 63. a-nongst 55 persons whom they consi lend deserving, sc.:lording to the intentism of the do oors.

RIVERS POLLUTION ACT.

Mr. H. Potts, clerk to the County Council, wrote on December 13th as follows :—Refarring to your letter of the Bth inst.,copy of which was forwarded to our Couni,y Medical Officer of Fleilth, I am inLrined by that official that he finds it a great difficulty to be more explicit than he was in his principal report with reference to your district. In that report you will observe it was represent: d that a large number of the brooks of the di s• trict had been so much polute i that they were made to do duty as sewers and that where so many streams are polluted with sewage, tannery waste, liquor, et., it is not easy to point out which streams are the foulest and most need attention, and that your Medieil Officer of Health and Nuisance Inspector are no doubt able to fur- nish your District Cemnod with that information inas- much as those officers are in the opinion of the County Medical Officer of Health well aware of the extent and nature of the pollution of the streams now going on in your district. I shall be glad. therefor?, by your fur- nishing me. for the information of our Rivers Pollution Committee,what action you propose taking for prevent- ing the streams being polluted. A Committee was appointed, consisting of the repre- sentatives of the districts in which the alleged ioffences were, to cons'der the mstter, and report. This was all the business.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SOCIAL EVENING AND SMOICER.—At the Ccdtiemative Club, Frodsham, on Wednesday night, an enjoyable smoking concert was held, presided over by Mr. A. Thomas. Songs and musical items were coatributed by a number of members. PUPIL TEACHERS' CENTRAL CLASsES..

The Committee, of Warrington and District Pupil Teachers' Day Central Classes have estab- lished classes for the higher education in secular work of pupil teachers, at considerable cost, in order to meet the requirements of the Education Department. A suitable large room at Sf;.Clement's dission has been rented, a highly qualified and ex- perienced first class certificated master and first class mistress have been engaged for the work; and new apparatus will be provided. An appeal is being made to ask foe liberal support in helping to defray the first cost of this worthy undertaking. The ex- penses are met,partly by fees,and aid grant,as well as School Manager's fees, but there will be a deficiency in the first year's working of £2OO. Provision will be made for a hundred pupil teachers (including Scholarship Class) from all schools of whatever denomination, and already fifty have joined the classes. Mr. E. K. Dennison B.A. (London) formerly of St. Mark's College, London, and recently of Leeds and Oldham P.T. Central Classes, and Miss Warbur- ton, nf Pendleton, Manchester, and trained at the Warrington College, a highly qualified Mistress, have been appointed Headmaster and Mistress to take charge. The following gentlemen form the Committee :—Tne Revs. Canon Willis (chairman), Morley Stevenson, H. V. Pigot, J. Carson, John Yonge, Messrs. J. D. Buckton, A. J. Jolley, E. J. Guest, Councillor F. Monks, Edward Wallington, Miss Shaw and John Dewhurst (hon. secretary), Already the firm of Messrs. Monks Hall and Co., has seat a generous subscription of ..£22 23 to the Rev. Morley Stevenson, and with the cheque a very kind letter, approving of the committee's en- deavour to improve the education of those, who will become our future teachers in the country. The classes commence about the middle of January. and success is assured if all the pupil teachers join

HIGHLANDS. The Central News Inverness correspondent telegraphs that up to noon yesterday no trace had been obtained of Allan M'Allum, the alleged murderer of Constable King. There are now over 60 men engaged in the search. It is supposed that the murderer is hiding in a cave in the mountains, but the difficulty of obtaining fcod must compel him soon to abandon this hiding place. LA.TEST LOCAL WEATHER FORECAST. COLLIERY FATALITY AT LEIGH. Yesterday morning, ab-ut 8 30, John Westh.ad, 32,0 f Mealhousc-lane, Atherton, was taking a tub of coal out of his drawing place in the Wigan Coal and Iron Com- PanY's Sovereign pit, Leigh. when some tubs on the brow top came running down. THE RESUMED INQUEST.—THE VERDICr. The inquest concerning the loss or the liner Mohegan on the Cornish coast on October last, was resumed at S. Keverne yesterday. The Coroner stated that after the Board of Trade inquiry it was unnecessary to call evi- dence, but several jurors present commented strongly on the carelessness of the navigati in, to which was attribu- ted the responsibility for the disaster. Suggestions were made that the captain wilfully ran his ship on the rocks, but the Coroner strongly deprecated th's.

_ THE VERDICT. After a brief consultation the jury roturned a verdict that the victims were found dead, having met their deaths through drowning thtoogh the wreck due to care- lessness and irregular navigation. THE WARK CASE.

Tho petition praying for the release of Lieutenant Wark has already received 7,000 signatures in Wool- wich, and a larger number in Greenwich and other localities in the neighbour:mod. It is anticipated that the total number of signatures to the Woolwich petition will reach 12,000. Mr. E. Richardson, secretary of the Wark Release Gommittee at Woolwich, writes to con- tradict the statement that the Woolwich petition is be- ing prepared by Mr.C.F. Gill. This, he says, would be a breach of professional etiquette, and the cmamit'ee consider the statement damaging to their case.
